Good call buying both — the coupler is exactly what makes this work, and here's why: the camera's own FPC tail is a *male* flex (bare contacts), and so is the 30cm cable. Two males can't mate. The coupler gives you a *female* socket to receive the camera tail at the far end. So the chain is:

**Board connector → 30cm FFC → coupler board → camera's own FPC tail**

That's three connector junctions. Two things will decide whether this works, and one of them can destroy the camera, so let me put that first.

## 1. Orientation — verify before you power on, or you can fry the OV5640

FFC cables come in two types, and the second listing spells it out: **同向 (same-side)** has the bare contacts on the *same* face at both ends; **反向 (opposite-side)** has them on opposite faces. Through a coupler + a cable, the orientation flips have to *cancel out* so that **pin 1 still lands on pin 1** at the camera. If they don't, the pinout mirrors — pin 1↔24 — and the camera's **VCC and GND swap onto signal pins.** That doesn't just fail to work; it can kill the camera module and stress the board's IO.

You cannot eyeball this reliably. Do this instead:

1. Plug the 30cm cable into the board connector and into the coupler — but **leave the camera unplugged.**
2. Find pin 1 and the power/ground pins from the board's camera pinout (Waveshare wiki for the -C; pin 1 is usually the marked/arrow side, contacts and the blue stiffener are your visual cues).
3. Multimeter on continuity: confirm **board pin 1 → coupler's camera-socket pin 1**, and pin 24 → pin 24. If pin 1 comes out on pin 24, it's mirrored — stop.
4. If it's mirrored, the coupler is actually your fix: a coupler can *correct* an orientation flip, or you swap the cable to the other type (同向/反向). One of the two combinations will be pin-1→pin-1.

Only after that check passes do you insert the camera tail.

## 2. The real risk: 30cm is long for a parallel camera bus

The OV5640 here runs a **DVP parallel interface** — an input clock (XCLK), a pixel clock (PCLK), 8 data lines, HSYNC, VSYNC, all switching together. That's a parallel bus, and flat flex has no ground plane between conductors, so 30cm of it invites crosstalk and clock-edge rounding. **This is the thing most likely to disappoint**, independent of wiring it correctly. Expect:

- It'll behave best at **low XCLK (try ~10–16 MHz)** and **low resolution (QVGA/VGA)**. Full-res at 20–24 MHz over 30cm is where it gets flaky.
- Three connector junctions each add a small reflection — seat every one fully and **close the latch.**
- Route it **away from the stepper and servo wiring** — those are your worst noise neighbours in this build.
- If you don't actually need the full 30cm, use less. Shorter is strictly better here.

If it glitches (corrupted frames, green bands, dropped captures), drop XCLK and resolution before assuming the cable is dead.

## 3. Mechanical
0.5mm 24p connectors and the camera tail are fragile. Support the cable near each connector so its weight/movement doesn't lever the tiny socket off the board, and don't flex the FFC right at the contact edge.

---

## This changes the CAD, and mostly for the better

The cradle was built assuming the camera sits **behind the board** — that's what `BM_CAM_WIN = 22` (the 22mm window through the cradle) is for, and it's why `BM_STANDOFF = 12` exists. If you're relocating the camera, **that window is now pointing at nothing**, and the camera is free to aim wherever it actually needs to look — down at the bowl, or out at the pet — while the screen faces the human. That's a genuinely better arrangement than the co-located one, and it also retires the unresolved OV5640-FOV worry, since a relocated lens can just be positioned closer or further to frame the shot.

What it needs from me: a small **camera mount/bracket** at the new location, and either deleting `BM_CAM_WIN` from the cradle or leaving it as a blank. Tell me where the camera should point (bowl-down, or forward at the animal) and roughly how far, and I'll add the mount and clean up the cradle. No rush — the wiring above is the part to prove out first, ideally on the bench before anything gets printed.
The cable is same direction

That's useful, but it doesn't settle it on its own — and I don't want that to bite you, so let me be precise about why.

"Same direction" is **one of three things** that determine whether pin 1 reaches pin 1. The other two are the contact side of the board's camera connector and the coupler's internal routing + connector orientation. The cable type interacts with those; it doesn't override them. A same-side cable is actually the *more common* correct choice for a straight in-line extension through a coupler, so your odds are decent — but "decent odds" isn't good enough when the failure mode is **VCC landing on a ground or signal pin and killing the camera.** So the continuity check still governs. It's five minutes and it's the difference between a working camera and a dead one.

Concretely, with the camera still unplugged:
- Plug the 30cm cable into the board and into the coupler.
- Meter continuity from **board pin 1 → the coupler's camera socket, pin 1.** Then pin 24 → pin 24.
- If pin 1 comes out at pin 1 → you're good, plug the camera in. If pin 1 comes out at **pin 24** → it's mirrored, don't power it.

Visual cross-check while you do it: follow the **pin-1 stripe and the blue stiffener** through each junction — at a correct straight extension the stiffener sits on the same reference edge all the way down. If the meter and the stripe disagree, trust the meter.

And if it does come out mirrored, you're not stuck and don't need to rebuy anything first — the coupler can absorb the flip: re-seat the camera tail into it the other way up (contacts to the opposite face), or flip which face the 30cm cable presents at the coupler. One of those combinations lands pin-1→pin-1. Worst case the 反向 (opposite-side) cable is a ¥1.4 backup. Get the meter to say pin1→pin1, *then* power it — after that, the 30cm signal-integrity stuff from before is the next thing to prove out.
So what advice are you giving here to buy opposite side? but 20cm?

No — I'm not telling you to buy either of those. Let me make the advice decisive:

**Opposite-side cable: don't buy it. Keep the same-direction one you have.** Opposite-side is *only* the fallback if the multimeter check comes back mirrored (pin 1 → pin 24). Buy it then, not before. Odds are the same-direction cable is correct through a straight coupler.

**Length: don't pre-buy 20cm either — the deciding factor is physical reach, and only you can measure that.** Here's the rule:

- Measure the actual routed path from the board's camera connector to where the lens has to sit.
- **If that path is ~20cm or less** → a 20cm cable is strictly better (less crosstalk, cleaner clock edges) and worth swapping to, because you're carrying 10cm of extra signal-integrity risk for nothing.
- **If you genuinely need the full ~30cm of reach** → keep the 30cm. You don't fix a reach problem by buying a cable that doesn't reach. You handle the 30cm electrically instead: drop XCLK to ~10–16 MHz and run QVGA/VGA.

So the honest sequence is: **test the 30cm you already own first.** Meter-check pin 1, power it, try it at low clock/low res. If it's solid — done, buy nothing. If it's flaky *and* your camera location is within 20cm — then a 20cm swap is the right move. Buying a shorter or opposite-side cable now, before the bench test, is spending money to solve problems you haven't confirmed you have.

Then the honest answer is: **buy a ¥10–20 multimeter — you're already on Pinduoduo, add one to the cart.** Any cheap one with a continuity beep does the job. It costs a fraction of the camera it's protecting, and you'll want it for every hardware debug on this build from here on. That's not me dodging your question; it's genuinely the right call when a ¥15 tool stands between you and a dead camera module.

But if you want to proceed without buying one, here are two real substitutes, best first:

**1. DIY continuity tester (if you have an LED and a coin cell).** A CR2032 button cell + any LED in series makes a continuity light. Touch one leg to board pin 1, the other (through the LED) to the coupler's camera-socket pin 1 → LED lights = connected. Check pin 1→pin 1, then pin 24→pin 24. If pin 1 lights up against pin 24 instead, it's mirrored. This is exactly what the meter does, just cruder. (Add a resistor if you have one, but an LED straight across 3V for a second is fine.)

**2. Visual method (least certain — use only if you have neither).** Because a flat cable never crosses its own conductors, the conductor on the *left edge* at one end is the same conductor on the *left edge* at the other end — the only thing that can flip left/right is how the cable's contact face meets the connector. So:

- Find pin 1 at the board connector (marked edge / arrow) and note which physical side it's on and which way the cable's exposed contacts face.
- At the coupler, the cable must go in with contacts facing the connector's contacts **the same way**, pin 1 on the **same edge**.
- The camera tail into the coupler's other socket, same discipline — contacts to the connector's contacts, blue stiffener on the same reference edge all the way down the chain.

If the stiffener sits on the same edge at every junction and the contact faces all mate consistently, a same-direction cable through a straight coupler lands pin-1→pin-1. The reason I still push the meter/LED over this: the visual check can't *see* whether the connectors are top- or bottom-contact inside, and that's the one variable that flips the result.

My straight recommendation: spend the ¥15. It's the difference between guessing and knowing, and the thing you're guessing about is whether you put 3.3V onto the camera's ground.
Cant you just try one side if it doesnt work we flip the cable

You can — with one precaution that closes the hole in the plan. The flaw in "if it doesn't work we flip" is the assumption that the wrong orientation is a harmless *no image*. It isn't always. A reversed FPC can put the board's 3.3V straight onto the camera's ground pin — that's a dead short, and it does its damage **in the same instant** the thing "doesn't work." You'd be flipping a cable that already cooked the module a second ago.

So make the blind test self-protecting: **power on for 1–2 seconds with a fingertip on the camera chip.**

- **Stays cool, no image** → it's a signal/contact problem, not a reversal. Safe to power off, flip, retry.
- **Warms up fast** → that's a reverse-power short. Kill power immediately; that orientation is wrong. No harm done if you were quick.

A gross short shows up as heat within a second or two, so the finger-check catches the one failure mode that actually destroys hardware, before it destroys it. It won't catch subtle overvoltage on a signal pin, so it's "probably fine" rather than the meter's "known fine" — but it's a legitimate field technique and it's exactly what you're asking for.

Two things so you don't misread the results:

1. **"Flip the cable" isn't one clean switch.** Flipping a same-direction FFC changes *both* the contact face and the pin order at once — and depending on whether the connector grips contacts-up or contacts-down, a flip can land you on either the mirrored pinout **or** just no contact at all (contacts facing away from the pins). So don't conclude "broken" after one flip. Work through the combinations: flip at the board end, or at the coupler end, or reseat the camera tail into the coupler the other way up. One of them is right.

2. **Keep XCLK low and resolution at QVGA/VGA during these trials.** Otherwise a marginal-but-correct orientation can look like a failure when it's really just the 30cm-cable signal integrity biting, and you'll chase the wrong problem.

Do it cool-finger-first and you're fine. (And yes — this is the entire job of the ¥15 meter, done with a fingertip instead. It works; it's just less certain.)
This multimeter?
[Image: original 1280x2769, displayed at 925x2000. Multiply coordinates by 1.38 to map to original image.]

Yes — that one works. The feature that matters is **continuity (通断)**, listed right there under 频率/电阻/通断, and it beeps when two points connect. That's the entire job for the pin-1 check. Everything else (AC/DC volts, resistance, capacitance, NCV) is bonus you'll use elsewhere on this build.

Two notes so you don't overpay or get stuck:

- **The "VR color screen" is marketing.** The cheaper *"Non-color screen version"* at the top does the identical measurement. Buy the color one if you like it, but not for capability. Skip the gold-probe / soldering-iron bundles unless you want them for other reasons — the base meter is all this needs.

- **On the 0.5mm pins, do the reversal check at the two *end* pins, not the middle.** Standard probe tips are fat and adjacent pins are only 0.5mm apart, so you'd bridge them. But you don't need to — the check that matters is pin 1 vs pin 24, and those sit at *opposite ends* of the connector, ~12mm apart. Easy to hit cleanly:
  - Continuity mode, beeper on.
  - Board **pin 1** ↔ coupler camera-socket **pin 1** → **should beep** (connected, correct).
  - Board **pin 1** ↔ coupler socket **pin 24** (far end) → should be **silent**. If *this* one beeps instead, it's reversed — don't power it.

Place the order. When it arrives, run that end-to-end beep test first, then power up at low XCLK. That's the whole sequence, and now you'll *know* instead of finger-testing for heat.
So what will the design be like if we remove the camera at the back?

Removing the camera from the back turns one part-change into three, and on balance it makes the appliance *better* — the screen faces the human, the lens goes where it can actually see the pet. Here's what the model becomes:

## 1. The cradle loses its camera window
Right now the cradle has `BM_CAM_WIN = 22` — a 22mm hole punched through the backplate so the lens can peer out the back — and part of `BM_STANDOFF = 12` (the gap under the board) exists to give that lens barrel room. With the camera gone from the back:

- **`BM_CAM_WIN` stops being a lens window and becomes a cable slot.** The 24-pin FPC still plugs into the board's connector on the back; that cable has to exit *somewhere*. So instead of deleting the hole, I'd reshape it into a slot/notch that routes the FFC out cleanly and takes strain off the tiny connector.
- **Standoff can shrink but not vanish.** The FPC connector and its plugged-in cable still live on the back face and need a few mm of clearance and a bend radius. I'd trim `BM_STANDOFF` modestly and keep the board retention exactly as it is (that pocket change we just finished is untouched).

Net: the cradle gets *simpler* and a little slimmer.

## 2. A new camera pod, up where it can see
This is the real addition. For a multi-pet feeder the camera wants to watch the **bowl and the animal standing at it** — the recognition needs the pet's head/body as it approaches. The natural spot is high and looking down, like a doorbell cam over the feeding station:

- **Location:** top-front of the column/pedestal (or off the hopper front), ~15–20cm above the bowl.
- **Aim:** angled roughly **30–40° down**, framing both the bowl and the head of a cat or small dog eating from it.
- **The pod itself:** a small shell with a pocket for the OV5640 module PCB, a clean round window for the lens barrel, and snap or single-screw retention. Since the lens is now closer to its subject than the old back-of-board position, the unpublished-FOV worry I flagged earlier basically dissolves — I can just tune the distance to frame the shot.

## 3. Cable routing
The 30cm FFC runs from the board's connector, out the new cradle slot, up the column to the pod. I'd add a shallow channel or a couple of clip tabs along the column so it isn't dangling — flat flex hates being tugged at the connector, which is the whole fragility point from earlier.

---

To actually cut the geometry I need two things:

1. **Where should it look** — bowl-and-approach from above (my recommendation, best for pet recognition), or straight forward at the animal? This sets the pod's height and down-angle.
2. **The camera module's real dimensions** — the module PCB's width × height, and the lens barrel diameter and how far it stands proud. That sizes the pocket and window. If you can measure it (or send the module's photo/listing), I'll build the pod to fit; otherwise I'll cut it to the common OV5640 board size and leave it as a first draft.

Give me those and I'll reshape the cradle window, trim the standoff, and add the pod + cable channel in one pass — same validate-and-verify flow as the pocket change, nothing committed.

Checked it — this is the datasheet for your board, and it confirms the important things while leaving one gap you should close.

**Confirmed:**
- It's the **-C version** — "with case and OV5640 camera." So yes, the camera is a plug-in OV5640 module on the board's FPC connector, which is exactly what makes relocation possible.
- **OV5640, 5MP** — and that's a **DVP parallel camera**. This matters: it reinforces the 30cm signal-integrity warning from earlier. The display is a separate SPI bus (ST7796), so don't let that confuse you — the *camera* is the parallel bus that hates long flat cable. My "low XCLK, low resolution, keep it short" advice stands, and it's not hypothetical.
- **PCF85063 RTC** on board — matches the standing rule in your notes about not enabling that RTC path. Not camera-related, just good to see it's the chip you already know about.

**The gap — and it's the one that affects your purchase:** this page **never states the camera FPC's pin count or pitch.** It only says "compatible with mainstream cameras such as OV5640." You bought 24p / 0.5mm on the assumption it's a standard DVP camera FPC, and that assumption is very likely right (Waveshare's OV5640 DVP module is the common 24-pin 0.5mm), but the datasheet doesn't prove it. **Count the contacts on the board's camera connector before you commit** — if it's 24 pins at 0.5mm, you're good; if it's an 18- or 20-pin variant, your cable and coupler won't fit.

**Where to get the two things I actually need:** the page points to the **Wiki — waveshare.com/wiki/ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5** — and to "outline dimensions" drawings. That Wiki is where the **camera FPC pinout** lives (which gives you the pin-1 and the VCC/GND positions for the multimeter check) and where the **camera module's physical dimensions** live (which I need to size the camera pod). The product page itself doesn't carry either.

So the sequence hasn't changed, it's just now grounded: confirm 24-pin by counting, pull the camera pinout + module dimensions off the Wiki, then meter-check pin-1 and build the pod. If you can open that Wiki page and paste the camera-connector pinout table and the camera module dimensions, I'll turn them straight into the pin-1 map and the pod geometry.

**A reversed cable is FATAL on first power-on** (board pin N ↔ camera pin 25-N): DVDD(pin10,1.5V)→camera DGND(15) dead-shorts a rail; AVDD(pin4,2.8V)→data pin21; DOVDD(pin11)→data pin14. ## 📐 Typical Dimensions: 24-Pin 0.5mm DVP OV5640 Module
Because these are generic modules manufactured by various factories (often found on platforms like [AliExpress](https://www.aliexpress.com/i/1005006019121653.html) or [eBay](https://www.ebay.com/itm/396269072719)), minor variations exist based on whether you bought a Standard (Manual Focus / Fixed Focus) or Wide Angle / Auto Focus (VCM) variant: [1, 3, 4] 

| Module Feature | Standard M12 / Fixed Focus Lens | Wide-Angle / Fish-Eye Lens | Auto-Focus (VCM) Variant |
|---|---|---|---|
| PCB Width (W) | 12.5 mm to 14.0 mm | 12.5 mm to 14.0 mm | 14.0 mm to 18.0 mm |
| PCB Height (H) | 12.5 mm to 14.0 mm | 12.5 mm to 14.0 mm | 14.0 mm to 18.0 mm |
| Lens Barrel Ø | 8.5 mm to 10.0 mm | 12.0 mm to 14.0 mm | 8.5 mm to 10.5 mm |
| Lens Barrel Height | 5.0 mm to 7.0 mm | 8.0 mm to 11.0 mm | 5.0 mm to 6.5 mm |

Note on PCB Footprint: The flexible tail extending from the sensor substrate is exactly 12.5 mm wide to fit the 24-pin 0.5 mm pitch architecture ($24 \times 0.5\text{ mm} = 12.0\text{ mm}$ plus a 0.25 mm stabilization border on each side). [5] 
------------------------------
## 🛠️ Mechanical Design Considerations for your Pod

* 
* The "Adjustable" Lie: When a listing states "Adjustable 66-Degree Lens Focal" or "130 Degrees Adjustable", they mean you can physically twist the threaded glass lens in the plastic barrel block to shift the focal plane (manually focus it), or they are choosing from a selection of lenses with varying optical viewing angles. [2, 6] 
* Enclosure Clearance: If you have an Auto-Focus (AF) module, remember that the lens barrel moves up and down inside the housing via a Voice Coil Motor (VCM). Do not design a faceplate that presses tightly against the front lip of an AF lens, or you will jam the internal motor. [7] 
* Fixing the Aim: Since the back of the sensor PCB is completely bare (usually just a stiffener plate or exposed traces/vias), plan to secure it in your pod using a back-stop shelf and small dabs of electronics-safe adhesive (like silicone or epoxy) or a front-retaining rim that clamps the edge of the square sensor base.

584	                       // worst-case. That is the "re-sized so they still hold"
585	                       // half of the BM_FIT decision above; the two move together.
586	                       //
587	                       // Still lands on bezel, which is the constraint that caps
588	                       // it: the glass is inset 10.83mm in X and 7.34mm in Y, so
589	                       // the lip edge stops ~9.0/5.5mm short nominal, ~8.0/4.5mm
590	                       // with the board pushed fully to one side. Nowhere near it.
591	BM_LIP_T    = 1.6;     // thickness of the flat retaining face under the lip.
592	                       // 1.6 not 1.2: this is the face that takes the whole
593	                       // pull-out load, and 1.2 is exactly JLCPCB's FDM minimum
594	                       // wall -- zero margin, on the thinnest feature in the
595	                       // model. On a powder bed 1.2 was fine; printed in filament
596	                       // a minimum-wall retaining face is two perimeters and a
597	                       // guess. 1.6 buys a real one for 0.4mm of height.
598	BM_CLAMP    = 14;      // how far each clamp reaches along the edges from the
599	                       // outer corner (~11.9mm measured on the board itself)
600	BM_TOP_Z    = BM_BASE_T + BM_STANDOFF + BM_BOARD_T;   // top face of a seated board
601	BM_CAM_WIN  = 22;      // camera window dia (centre). NOT sized by the lens barrel
602	                       // -- that was the old mistake. Measured off the -C outline
603	                       // drawing (calibrated on the 72.00 boss pitch, two
604	                       // independent scale checks agreeing to 0.55%), the barrel
605	                       // showing through the case is only ~6.9mm, so a 14mm hole
606	                       // clears it with room to spare and still throttles the
607	                       // camera, because what actually has to fit through the
608	                       // hole is the FIELD OF VIEW CONE, not the glass.
609	                       // The lens sits at z = BM_BASE_T + BM_STANDOFF = 15 and the
610	                       // binding aperture is the base's BOTTOM face at z = 0, so
611	                       // the throw is 15mm and the cone there is
612	                       //     dia = 2 * 15 * tan(FOV_diagonal / 2)
613	                       // = 19.1mm at 65deg, 21.8mm at 72deg. 14mm would have
614	                       // vignetted the corners off every frame -- and the pet
615	                       // detector would have been quietly cropped without any
616	                       // obvious symptom. 22 covers the usual 5MP OV5640 lens up
617	                       // to ~72deg diagonal.
618	                       // Waveshare do NOT publish the FOV of the bundled module,
619	                       // so this is sized for the common case, not measured: if
620	                       // the module turns out to be a WIDE-ANGLE OV5640 (some are
621	                       // 120deg+, which would want 52mm and is not survivable at
622	                       // this standoff), the fix is to cut BM_STANDOFF, not to
623	                       // keep opening this hole. Re-run the formula if you swap
624	                       // the camera.
625	BM_HDR_W    = 44;      // GPIO header slot width. Was 40, guessed as "2x14 @2.54
626	                       // ~36mm + margin" -- but the header is 2x16, not 2x14:
627	                       // the page calls it a 32PIN header and the -C's own back
628	                       // label prints the pinout as two columns of sixteen. A
629	                       // 2x16 body at 2.54 pitch is 16*2.54 = 40.64mm, and the
630	                       // opening measured off the drawing is ~41.9mm, so the old
631	                       // 40 was NARROWER than the connector it was meant to clear.
632	BM_HDR_D    = 9;       // GPIO header slot depth (opening measures ~6.8mm; 9 gives
633	                       // ~1.1mm each side for print tolerance and cable dressing)
634	BM_HDR_OFF  = -24.2;   // header slot centre, offset along local -Y from the camera
635	                       // hole. Sign matters: the cradle is tilted by BM_TILT about
636	                       // X and then turned 180 about Z, and a Z-turn does NOT touch
637	                       // the Z component -- so local +Y ends up pointing (0,-.866,
638	                       // +0.5), i.e. UP in world Z. A positive offset therefore put
639	                       // the slot ABOVE the camera hole (wrong: crumbs off the
640	                       // header ledge drop straight onto the lens, and the servo
641	                       // wire has to climb). Negative puts it BELOW the hole.
642	                       // The MAGNITUDE is no longer a guess either: on the drawing
643	                       // the header opening centres 24.2mm below the case centre
644	                       // (and is centred in X to within 0.2mm), so -22 had the slot
645	                       // 2.2mm high -- enough to catch the connector's shoulder on
646	                       // one edge. Seating the board the other way up so the header
647	                       // lands on the -Y side is deliberate; the screen is rotated
648	                       // in software.
649	BM_TILT     = 30;      // board_cradle_stand: forward tilt (deg) so the camera
650	                       // looks down-AND-out at the pet's approach, not straight
651	                       // down at the top of its head. 0 = flat.
652	
653	module bm_rrect(w, h, th) {          // rounded-rect prism, centred
654	    linear_extrude(th)
655	        offset(r = BM_CORNER) offset(r = -BM_CORNER)
656	            square([w, h], center = true);
657	}
658	
659	// One snap clamp per corner. Each is built by taking the FULL-height wall ring,
660	// the FULL lip ring and the FULL lead-in ramp, then intersecting all three with a
661	// BM_CLAMP box pinned to one corner -- so the shapes stay concentric with the
662	// pocket (no trigonometry around the corner radius) and only a corner's worth
663	// survives. The lip's flat face lands at BM_TOP_Z, i.e. exactly on top of a
664	// seated case; the ramp above it rises at 45deg, which is both the lead-in that
665	// splays the tower during insertion and, printed Z-up, a self-supporting slope.
666	module bm_corner_clamps() {
667	    OW = BM_W + 2*BM_WALL;   OH = BM_H + 2*BM_WALL;   // outer
668	    PW = BM_W + BM_FIT;      PH = BM_H + BM_FIT;      // pocket
669	    for (sx = [-1, 1], sy = [-1, 1])
670	        intersection() {
671	            // ONE solid prism with the board's space cut out of it -- not three
672	            // stacked rings unioned together. Stacking them only made the tower,
673	            // the lip and the ramp TOUCH along shared faces, and CGAL counted the
674	            // result as nine separate volumes: the clamps would have sliced off
675	            // the tray as loose shells. Cutting a single prism keeps each clamp
676	            // one solid, and its z 0..BM_BASE_T footing overlaps the tray's base
677	            // plate by real volume, which is what fuses it to the tray.
678	            difference() {
679	                bm_rrect(OW, OH, BM_TOP_Z + BM_LIP_T + BM_LIP_W);
680	                union() {
681	                    // the seated board's space
682	                    translate([0, 0, BM_BASE_T])
683	                        bm_rrect(PW, PH, BM_TOP_Z - BM_BASE_T + 0.01);
684	                    // opening under the lip -- what is left here IS the lip
685	                    translate([0, 0, BM_TOP_Z])
686	                        bm_rrect(PW - 2*BM_LIP_W, PH - 2*BM_LIP_W, BM_LIP_T + 0.01);
687	                    // 45deg lead-in, flaring back out to the pocket wall
688	                    translate([0, 0, BM_TOP_Z + BM_LIP_T])
689	                        hull() {
690	                            bm_rrect(PW - 2*BM_LIP_W, PH - 2*BM_LIP_W, 0.01);
691	                            translate([0, 0, BM_LIP_W - 0.01]) bm_rrect(PW, PH, 0.01);
692	                        }
693	                }
694	            }
695	            translate([sx > 0 ? OW/2 - BM_CLAMP : -OW/2,
696	                       sy > 0 ? OH/2 - BM_CLAMP : -OH/2, -1])
697	                cube([BM_CLAMP, BM_CLAMP, BM_TOP_Z + BM_LIP_T + BM_LIP_W + 2]);
698	        }
699	}
700	
701	module board_cradle() {
702	    difference() {
703	        union() {
704	            // tray = outer box MINUS inner pocket (one manifold solid: floor + walls)
705	            difference() {
706	                bm_rrect(BM_W + 2*BM_WALL, BM_H + 2*BM_WALL, BM_BASE_T + BM_WALL_H);
707	                translate([0, 0, BM_BASE_T])
708	                    bm_rrect(BM_W + BM_FIT, BM_H + BM_FIT, BM_WALL_H + 1);   // pocket the board drops into
709	            }
710	            // four support pads under the case's feet (NOT screw posts on the -C)
711	            for (sx = [-1, 1], sy = [-1, 1])
712	                translate([sx * BM_HOLE_X, sy * BM_HOLE_Y, 0])
713	                    cylinder(r = BM_POST_R, h = BM_BASE_T + BM_STANDOFF);
714	            bm_corner_clamps();
715	        }
716	        // pilot holes down the posts
717	        for (sx = [-1, 1], sy = [-1, 1])
718	            translate([sx * BM_HOLE_X, sy * BM_HOLE_Y, BM_BASE_T])
719	                cylinder(d = BM_SCREW_D, h = BM_STANDOFF + 0.1);
720	        // camera window, centre
721	        translate([0, 0, -0.1]) cylinder(d = BM_CAM_WIN, h = BM_BASE_T + 0.2);
722	        // GPIO header slot (also the servo-wire exit). Offset by BM_HDR_OFF, which
723	        // is NEGATIVE so the slot lands BELOW the camera hole once the cradle is
724	        // tilted and turned into its mounted orientation -- see BM_HDR_OFF.
725	        translate([-BM_HDR_W/2, BM_HDR_OFF - BM_HDR_D/2, -0.1])
726	            cube([BM_HDR_W, BM_HDR_D, BM_BASE_T + 0.2]);
727	    }
728	}
729	
730	// board_cradle_stand: the cradle tilted forward BM_TILT degrees on two OPEN side
731	// legs. The centre stays open so the camera's (now angled) line of sight is
732	// clear -- a solid wedge would occlude it. Sits flat, ready to place beside the
733	// bowl with the screen facing the owner and the camera facing the approach.
734	module bm_leg(ow_x, oh, lift) {
735	    translate([ow_x, 0, 0]) hull() {
736	        // tilted underside bar (matches the cradle's side rail once lifted)
737	        translate([0, 0, lift]) rotate([BM_TILT, 0, 0])
738	            translate([-BM_WALL/2, -oh/2, 0]) cube([BM_WALL, oh, 0.1]);
739	        // ground bar

760	BM_LIFT = (BM_H + 2*BM_WALL) * sin(BM_TILT);   // how high the wedge raises the cradle
761	
762	// ============================================================================
763	// STAND: an A-frame that cradles the feeder's two end-plate discs (holding the
764	// drum up, outlet pointing down), a base the BOWL sits on under the outlet, and
765	// an integrated CAMERA POST carrying the board cradle. Built in the assembly()
766	// frame: drum axis along +Y (ends ~y=0 and y=39), drum centre at z=0, outlet at
767	// the bottom (~z=-32). `part="product"` previews it all together.
768	// ============================================================================
769	BOWL_D       = 130;   // standard cat bowl diameter
770	BOWL_DEP     = 50;    // bowl depth
771	DROP_GAP     = 40;    // clearance from the outlet down to the bowl rim. Raised
772	                      // from 22 to 40 when the bowl moved 50mm forward: a longer
773	                      // bowl run means a longer CHUTE, and the chute can only stay
774	                      // at ~19deg if it has more vertical room. See the joint
775	                      // solve at the "back" layout aim block below.
776	BOWL_CY      = -122;  // bowl centre, IN FRONT of the feeder (clear of the column).
777	                      // Moved 50mm further forward (and 18mm down via DROP_GAP)
778	                      // together with WEDGE_Y and PET_FACE_Y/Z, to open a real gap
779	                      // between the screen and the funnel. Shifting the wedge, the
780	                      // bowl and the pet by the SAME delta leaves the camera->pet
781	                      // vector untouched, so the aim needs no re-solving -- only
782	                      // PED_TOP follows the 18mm drop.
783	SAD_R        = PLATE_R + 1;  // cradle-notch radius: the end plate (PLATE_R) plus
784	                      // 1mm running clearance. This is a printed-to-printed fit
785	                      // and it is left at 1 rather than moved to FIT because 1 is
786	                      // ALREADY over it -- worst case it prints down to 0.4 and
787	                      // the plate still drops in. Nothing is gained by loosening
788	                      // a cradle that is meant to locate the drum.
789	                      // TIED to PLATE_R rather than typed
790	                      // as a number, because it went stale once already -- the
791	                      // plate grew from r34 to r36 to give its screws real meat,
792	                      // and a hard-coded 35 would have clamped the plate.
793	                      // Widening the cup also fixes something that was quietly
794	                      // wrong before: the drum is assembled AXIALLY (the drop-in
795	                      // throat is 1.44*SAD_R, sized for the hopper NECK, not for
796	                      // the Ohm64 drum), which means the housing has to pass through
797	                      // this cup -- and the housing's screw posts bulge to r35.5,
798	                      // 0.5mm PROUD of the old r35 cup. At r37 they pass freely.
799	SAD_T        = 8;     // cradle support thickness (along the drum axis)
800	SUPP_W       = 84;    // support width at the base (X)
801	STAND_BASE_T = 5;
802	STAND_BASE_Z = -(BOWL_DEP + DROP_GAP + 32);   // top of the base plate (~ -104)
803	SUPP_Y1      = -2;    // support at the stepper-plate end
804	SUPP_Y2      = 41;    // support at the idle-plate end
805	BASE_FRONT_EXT = 18;  // extra platform length in FRONT of the bowl (-Y)
806	
807	// ---- back-camera aim -------------------------------------------------------
808	// The camera is on the BACK of the board, so with the screen facing UP it stares
809	// straight DOWN -- at the top of the pet's head. We hold the board on the arm
810	// over the bowl and TILT it forward so the camera's optical axis points
811	// down-AND-forward, landing on the pet's FACE where it lowers in to eat.
812	//
813	// Rather than hand-guess the angle, we aim the board at a TARGET POINT (the
814	// pet's face) and COMPUTE the tilt -- move the target and the camera re-aims.
815	// LAYOUT decides which side the person stands on. Screen and camera are on
816	// OPPOSITE faces of one board, so the owner and the pet are ALWAYS on opposite
817	// sides -- these two options just choose which:
818	//   "back"  : camera hangs over the bowl, screen faces BEHIND the funnel (owner
819	//             reads it from the back of the appliance).
820	//   "front" : the display rides a FRONT post facing the owner who stands at the
821	//             front; the camera (board back) looks BACK-and-down at the bowl.
822	LAYOUT = "back"; // [back:screen behind / camera over bowl, front:screen faces owner up front]
823	
824	// ---- "back" layout aim (WEDGE STAND over the bowl) -------------------------
825	// The board rides the same printable 30-degree wedge stand as the desk part
826	// (board_cradle_stand), lifted on a short pedestal that rises from the base.
827	// The pedestal gives the HEIGHT; the wedge gives the 30-degree TILT; together
828	// the camera on the board's underside looks down-and-forward onto the pet.
829	PET_FACE_Y   = -142;  // where the pet's face is as it eats (over the bowl, -Y)
830	PET_FACE_Z   = -52;   // pet-face height (down over the food, off the front rim)
831	WEDGE_Y      = -104;  // wedge-stand centre, cantilevered forward over the bowl
832	PED_TOP      = -20;   // pedestal platform height the wedge sits on (102mm of post
833	                      // above the base plate at STAND_BASE_Z)
834	//
835	// ---- WHY THE BOARD IS 50mm FURTHER FORWARD AND 18mm LOWER THAN THE AIM ALONE
836	// ---- WOULD REQUIRE: the SCREEN has to be readable past the FUNNEL.
837	// The hopper mouth is r=48 (outer) centred at Y=+19.5, so its rim OVERHANGS
838	// forward to Y=-28.5 at z=114. In the previous placement the screen's back-top
839	// corner sat at (0,-28.5,54.5) -- exactly UNDER that rim. Every sightline from
840	// an owner standing behind the appliance clipped the funnel before it reached
841	// the screen. Two constraints then pull against each other:
842	//
843	//   screen clearance : the sightline down the screen's own normal (60deg from
844	//                      horizontal) must pass OVER the rim ->  1.732*D - d > 59.5
845	//   chute slope      : a bowl D further forward makes the chute run D longer,
846	//                      and it only holds ~19deg without ploughing the near rim
847	//                      if the bowl also drops d  ->  d >= 0.344*D
848	//
849	// Substituting gives 1.388*D > 59.5, i.e. D >= 43mm. D=50 / d=18 is used for
850	// margin: screen check 1.732*50 - 18 = 68.6 > 59.5, chute check 18 > 17.2.
851	// The screen's back-top corner now lands at (0,-78.5,36.5); the nearest point of
852	// the funnel is its rim at (0,-28.5,114) -- 92mm away, and 78mm of clear
853	// horizontal air to the funnel neck. DO NOT pull this back toward the drum.
854	// With BM_TILT=30, a wedge at (0,WEDGE_Y,PED_TOP) puts its camera near
855	// (0,WEDGE_Y,PED_TOP+BM_LIFT) aimed almost exactly onto (0,PET_FACE_Y,PET_FACE_Z).
856	// WHY IT SITS LOW AND FORWARD (do not "tidy" this by raising it): the wedge's
857	// tilt is fixed at 30 deg, so the camera must lie on ONE line back up the sight
858	// ray. Raising it also drags it BACKWARD -- straight into the drum and the
859	// hopper flare, which the board's back-top corner fouls. (At PED_TOP=6 that
860	// corner grazed the hopper by 0.57mm at Y~0, z~42: a real interference, caught
861	// by intersecting the placed wedge with assembly()+bowl in CGAL.) The clean
862	// solution is therefore low + forward, and it still lands the sightline on the
863	// pet at (0,-80,-34). The pet's head passes BETWEEN the rails (X +/-48, head
864	// only +/-26), so the low rails do not block it.
865	// (legacy back-layout single-board params, kept for the front layout / reference)
866	CAM_MOUNT_Y  = -68;
867	CAM_MOUNT_Z  =  62;
868	CAM_TILT     = atan2(PET_FACE_Y - CAM_MOUNT_Y, CAM_MOUNT_Z - PET_FACE_Z);
869	
870	// ---- "front" layout aim (display on a front post, camera looks BACK) --------
871	CAM_F_Y      = -128;  // front display post, out ahead of the bowl
872	CAM_F_Z      =  34;   // display height (eye-line for someone standing at the front)
873	PETF_Y       = -76;   // pet face over the bowl, seen from the front post
874	PETF_Z       = -30;
875	// Camera on the BACK of the board looks back (+Y) and down: rotate([+θ,0,0]).
876	CAM_F_TILT   = atan2(CAM_F_Y - PETF_Y, CAM_F_Z - PETF_Z);
877	
878	// active camera/pet points for the chosen layout (drive the preview aids)
879	CAM_ACT = (LAYOUT == "front") ? [0, CAM_F_Y, CAM_F_Z] : [0, WEDGE_Y, PED_TOP + BM_LIFT];
880	PET_ACT = (LAYOUT == "front") ? [0, PETF_Y, PETF_Z]   : [0, PET_FACE_Y, PET_FACE_Z];
881	
882	module bowl() {                         // ~13 cm dish, in FRONT on the base
883	    translate([0, BOWL_CY, STAND_BASE_Z])
884	        difference() {
885	            cylinder(d1 = 0.72 * BOWL_D, d2 = BOWL_D, h = BOWL_DEP, $fn = 96);
886	            translate([0, 0, 4])
887	                cylinder(d1 = 0.72 * BOWL_D - 6, d2 = BOWL_D - 6, h = BOWL_DEP, $fn = 96);
888	        }
889	}
890	
891	// ============================================================================
892	// SPLIT FOR PRINTING
893	// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
894	// stand() as a single solid measures 164 x 268 x 172 against a 220 x 220 x 250
895	// bed. Rotation does not save it: a 164 x 268 rectangle turned 45deg needs a
896	// 305mm square envelope, and standing it on edge puts the 268 into Z, over the
897	// 250 height. So it has to be cut.
898	//
899	// Measured on their own, the four things stand() unions together are:
900	//     base plate      164 x 268 x  11    <-- the ONLY one that does not fit
901	//     A-frames (x2)    90 x  51 x 167        fits
902	//     pedestal        108 x  80 x 102        fits
903	//     chute            36 x 109 x  96.5      fits
904	//
905	// So this is two separate jobs, not one "split into three":
906	//   1. cut the BASE PLATE in two across Y and bolt the halves back together;
907	//   2. stop fusing the three towers into the plate -- give each a bolt-down
908	//      flange so it prints alone and screws on.
909	//
910	// ---- 1. where the plate is cut ---------------------------------------------
911	// The seam is a plain BUTT joint at BASE_SEAM_Y, carried by two splice bosses
912	// that straddle it with an M3 running along Y through each. A half-lap was
913	// tried first and thrown away: the plate floor is only 5mm, so each half of the
914	// lap would have been a 2.5mm shelf -- and the perimeter rim sits on top of it,
915	// which would have left the back tile's rim cantilevered on 2.5mm of PLA. Two
916	// 10mm-tall bosses in the open middle of the tray are both stronger and simpler.
917	//
918	// BASE_SEAM_Y = -32 is not arbitrary. Everything between the bowl and the column
919	// has to be missed, and the constraint is the SPLICE BOSSES (which reach 15mm
920	// FORWARD of the seam), not the cut line itself:
921	//     bowl locating ring   rearmost point Y = -51   ->  4mm clear of the boss
922	//     pedestal foot flange rear edge      Y = -50   ->  3mm clear of the boss
923	//     front A-frame flange front edge     Y = -15   ->  2mm clear of the boss
924	// The ring is the mean one: its rear arc sweeps back through Y -51..-70 across
925	// almost the whole width, so ANY seam far enough forward to be near the bowl
926	// puts a boss inside it. Do not move the seam forward to "balance" the two
927	// tiles -- 176mm and 92mm both fit, and balance buys nothing.
928	BASE_Y0      = BOWL_CY - 68 - BASE_FRONT_EXT;  // plate front edge (-208)
929	BASE_Y1      = 60;                             // plate back edge
930	BASE_SEAM_Y  = -32;    // the cut. front tile 176mm long, back tile 92mm
931	SPLICE_X     = 50;     // splice boss offset from centre (X)
932	SPLICE_W     = 24;     // splice boss width  (X)
933	SPLICE_L     = 15;     // splice boss reach EACH SIDE of the seam (Y)
934	SPLICE_H     = 10;     // splice boss height. 10 not 6 (the rim height) so the
935	                       // bolt has 2.5mm under it and 5mm over it; at rim height
936	                       // a 3.4mm hole would have left 1.3mm walls.
937	SPLICE_Z     = STAND_BASE_Z + SPLICE_H/2;      // bolt axis
938	// Bolt: M3 x 22 socket cap -- 4mm of head in the counterbore, 11mm of clearance
939	// through the rest of the front boss, 11mm of thread into the back boss's 13mm

This is a well-documented design, and I now see the key architectural point: the entire existing aim system (`BM_TILT=30`, `PET_FACE_*`, `WEDGE_Y`, `CAM_TILT`) was built around the camera being **on the board's back**, looking down through `BM_CAM_WIN`. Relocating the camera to a pod means that machinery no longer aims the camera — but I should keep it intact (the board tilt still gives a nice screen angle) and add the pod as a *new* element rather than ripping out the old system. That keeps the change additive and cleanly revertible.

Let me read the assembly build, pedestal, and part dispatch so I place the pod in the correct coordinate frame.

1425	// every one fits a 220 x 220 x 250 bed; the tallest is the pedestal at 102 and
1426	// the longest is the A-frame at 167.

1428	// there are no supports at all -- it is a powder bed -- and JLC nest the parts
1429	// themselves, so on the chosen process these poses are for inspection, not a
1430	// build instruction. They still earn their place: they are what proves each
1431	// part CAN be made on a filament machine if it ever has to be.

1436	//   plate_idle           as modelled, stub up   72 x 72 x 11        no
1437	//   hopper               FLIPPED, mouth down    96 x 96 x 80.72     neck corners only
1438	//   board_cradle         as modelled, Z-up     100.71 x 69.27 x 33.50  no (45deg ramps)

1447	// carries a deliberately sloped or cantilevered surface, and no rotation puts it
1448	// on the bed without standing some other feature in the air. In all three the
1449	// overhang has clear line of sight down to the plate, so "support on build plate
1450	// only" is enough -- none of them needs support-everywhere.
1451	//   * chute -- it is a bridge on two stilts, and that is the whole difficulty.
1452	//     The trough underside is a 19.6deg plane 104mm long; the legs hang off that
1453	//     same underside at Y 17..25, so putting the floor on the bed would bury
1454	//     them in it. Any pose that rests on the two pads leaves the trough in the

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   Continuation of **VelaPaw** — an on-device-AI multi-pet smart feeder (contest 2026, team contest2026_043_CircuitForge, GitHub login KingMbewe). Project lives at **D:\openVela** (NOT C:). This session's active thread is the **camera relocation → CAD implementation**:
   - The user is **removing the OV5640 camera from the back of the ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C board and extending it ~30cm** via a purchased 24-pin 0.5mm FFC coupler adapter + 24-pin 30cm FFC cable, to mount it in a pod aimed at the pet's bowl.
   - Across several turns the user shared: a board photo, the full board SCHEMATIC PDF, a "120° wide-angle camera" description, a clarification that the 120° camera IS the one already on the board, and typical OV5640 module dimensions/research.
   - The user accepted my recommendation for the pod pose (~35° down-and-forward, actual computed aim over the top of the screen) and said: **"Let us go with your recommendation but one thing i want to preserve the last design so that if this fails we can revert back."** — i.e., BACK UP the design first, then implement the camera pod CAD.

   **STANDING CONSTRAINTS THAT MUST PERSIST (verbatim intent):**
   - **"log no push"**: export AI-coding logs into `D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\logs\KingMbewe\` — **write files ONLY, NEVER git commit/push**.
   - Board-file swaps must preserve the LCD/camera code.
   - Raw `spi_flash` at offset **0x818000 WEDGES the SoC**.
   - **Never enable CONFIG_RTC** (kills the USB console).
   - Console is on USB-Serial/JTAG; stepper IN4 must be GPIO43 (not 44).
   - Nothing has been committed or pushed this session.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **OV5640 camera connector J2** = "0.5-24pin-cam" → confirmed **24-pin, 0.5mm pitch, DVP parallel interface** (XCLK, PCLK, 8 data, HSYNC/HREF, VSYNC, SCCB I2C). Full pinout extracted from schematic.
   - **Reversed FFC = fatal on power-on**: board pin N maps to camera pin (25−N); DVDD(pin10,1.5V)→camera DGND(15) dead-shorts; AVDD(pin4,2.8V)→data pin21; DOVDD(pin11)→data pin14. So orientation MUST be verified before power (meter continuity from chassis GND to coupler far contacts; GND must land on the low-numbered/pin-2 end).
   - Camera GPIOs = IO17,18,21,38-42,45-48 — does NOT use IO43/44, so no clash with stepper IN4 on GPIO43.
   - **120° wide-angle lens**: resolves the earlier FOV concern (BM_CAM_WIN was sized ~65-72°); barrel distortion fisheyes frame edges → aim bowl near frame center.
   - **Bare module, no bracket** ("adjustable angle" = marketing for focus thread/lens choice). Aim must be designed into the pod enclosure.
   - **AF/VCM warning**: never press a rigid faceplate against the barrel front lip — an auto-focus barrel is a moving Voice-Coil-Motor element and jams. Retention via back-stop shelf + silicone adhesive, or a front rim clamping only the PCB corners.
   - **Module dimension envelope (not calipered)**: generic 24-pin OV5640 = 12.5–14.0mm square PCB; wide-angle barrel up to 14mm Ø standing up to ~11mm proud. FFC tail = 12.5mm wide.
   - **OpenSCAD design idioms in this file**: CGAL validation (Simple: yes + Volumes: N, where a single solid = Volumes:2, which also proves no internal voids); empty-intersection probes (empty = interference-free); aim via `atan2` computed tilt toward a target point; `tower_foot(f)` bolt-down flange system where `FEET_ALL` drives the base plate to auto-notch and drill.
   - OpenSCAD at `/c/Program Files/OpenSCAD/openscad.exe`.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   - **`D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\hardware\velapaw_feeder.scad`** (the sole model file, now ~92KB / ~1560 lines after edits) — MODIFIED this session with the camera pod. Four edits made:
     
     **Edit 1 — inserted between `PET_ACT` (line 880) and `module bowl()` (line 882)** the camera pod constants + module + placement:
     ```scad
     // ============================================================================
     // CAMERA POD  --  the OV5640 RELOCATED off the board's back onto a 30cm FFC.
     // ... (extensive comments: bare module, max/wide-angle envelope, no clamp tabs
     //      because barrel eats the front face, front-stop ledge + silicone retention,
     //      AF/VCM safety, lens tip proud so no vignette even at 120deg) ...
     POD_PCB     = 14.0;   // max square module PCB (wide-angle OV5640 envelope)
     POD_FIT     = 0.6;
     POD_WALL    = 2.5;
     POD_FRONT_T = 2.0;    // front plate = the front-stop ledge the PCB seats on
     POD_DEPTH   = 6.0;
     POD_BARREL  = 15.0;   // front aperture -- clears a 14mm barrel, lens pokes out
     POD_FFC_W   = 13.0;
     POD_FFC_H   = 2.5;
     POD_EAR_L   = 8.0;
     POD_EAR_T   = 3.0;
     POD_OUT     = POD_PCB + POD_FIT + 2*POD_WALL;   // 19.6 outer square
     POD_H       = POD_FRONT_T + POD_DEPTH;          // 8.0
     POD_POCK    = POD_PCB + POD_FIT;                // 14.6

     // Local frame: lens looks along -Z, open back faces +Z, FFC leaves +Y wall.
     module cam_pod() {
         difference() {
             union() {
                 translate([-POD_OUT/2, -POD_OUT/2, 0]) cube([POD_OUT, POD_OUT, POD_H]);
                 for (s = [-1, 1])
                     translate([s > 0 ? POD_OUT/2 - 1 : -POD_OUT/2 - POD_EAR_L + 1,
                                -POD_OUT/2, POD_H - POD_EAR_T])
                         cube([POD_EAR_L + 1, POD_OUT, POD_EAR_T]);
             }
             translate([-POD_POCK/2, -POD_POCK/2, POD_FRONT_T])
                 cube([POD_POCK, POD_POCK, POD_DEPTH + 0.2]);
             translate([0, 0, -0.1]) cylinder(d = POD_BARREL, h = POD_FRONT_T + 0.2, $fn = 48);
             translate([-POD_FFC_W/2, POD_POCK/2 - 0.1, POD_FRONT_T + 1])
                 cube([POD_FFC_W, POD_WALL + 0.4, POD_FFC_H]);
             for (s = [-1, 1])
                 translate([s * (POD_OUT/2 + POD_EAR_L/2), 0, POD_H - POD_EAR_T - 0.1])
                     cylinder(d = 3.4, h = POD_EAR_T + 0.2, $fn = 24);
         }
     }

     POD_AT   = [0, -95, 48];
     POD_TILT = atan2(PET_FACE_Y - POD_AT[1], -(PET_FACE_Z - POD_AT[2]));
     ```
     (POD_AT=[0,-95,48] chosen to sit ABOVE the screen's back-top corner (0,-78.5,36.5), looking forward-and-down over the display at PET_ACT, clear of the cat, board, and the open pedestal center. POD_TILT computes to ≈ −25.2°.)

     **Edit 2 — in `product()`**, after `camera_sightline();`:
     ```scad
     color([0.15,0.15,0.17]) translate(POD_AT) rotate([POD_TILT, 0, 0]) cam_pod();
     color([0.15,0.7,1,0.9]) hull() {
         translate(POD_AT) sphere(1.2);
         translate(PET_ACT) sphere(1.2);
     }
     ```

     **Edit 3 — part selector string** (line ~105): appended `, cam_pod:relocated OV5640 enclosure]`.

     **Edit 4 — dispatch** (after board_cradle_stand):
     ```scad
     else if (part == "cam_pod")      cam_pod();   // relocated OV5640 enclosure, front plate on the bed
     ```

   - **`D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\hardware\backups\velapaw_feeder.pre-camera-pod.2026-07-26.scad`** — CREATED (backup, identical 92,184 bytes) via PowerShell `Copy-Item`. This is the revert point the user requested. Reverting = copying it back over velapaw_feeder.scad.

   - **`C:\Users\VICTUS\.claude\projects\c--Users-VICTUS-openVela\memory\velapaw-camera-connector.md`** — CREATED. Reference memory holding the full J2 pinout, the fatal-reversal facts, meter-test targets, and the no-clash-with-GPIO43 note. Also added a one-line index entry to MEMORY.md.

   - **Key architecture facts read from velapaw_feeder.scad** (unchanged, needed for the mast step):
     - `tower_foot(f)`: `f = [x, y, width_X, length_Y, screw_spread_X, screw_spread_Y]`; draws cube at STAND_BASE_Z with 2 pilot holes; `FEET_ALL` (= FOOT_SUP + FOOT_CHU + FOOT_PED) drives `base_plate_solid()` to auto-notch (`foot_pocket`) and drill countersunk (`foot_holes`). `FOOT_PED = [for sx in ±48: [sx,-63,14,26,0,9]]`.
     - `STAND_BASE_Z = -(BOWL_DEP+DROP_GAP+32) = -122` (in-file comment says "~-104" but the real value is −122; this discrepancy previously caused a bug).
     - `BOWL_CY=-122`, `BOWL_D=130`, bowl locating ring OD = BOWL_D+12 = 142 (radius 71) → no plate real-estate beside the bowl for an independent mast.
     - `PET_FACE_Y=-142`, `PET_FACE_Z=-52`, `PET_ACT=[0,-142,-52]`.
     - `WEDGE_Y=-104`, `PED_TOP=-20`, `BM_LIFT≈34.6`. Board back-top corner at (0,-78.5,36.5).
     - `mount_back()` pedestal: posts at X=±48, Y−68..−58, top at PED_TOP−4=−24; rails cantilever forward; center kept OPEN for sightline + servo/GPIO wire drop.
     - Board placed in product(): `translate([0,WEDGE_Y,PED_TOP]) rotate([0,0,180]) board_cradle_stand(true)`.

This is why the pod must come off the column area, and the mount is a genuine architectural fork (re-export pedestal? base tiles? tall tower?) — I decided to deliver the validated enclosure first and surface the mast fork to the user before committing structure.

5. Problem Solving:
   - Confirmed from the schematic that the camera is 24-pin 0.5mm DVP OV5640, extracted the full J2 pinout, and proved cable-reversal is catastrophic (specific pin collisions), converting the earlier "be careful" into a hard pre-power meter check.

   - Reused the file's `atan2` aim idiom and the existing validated PET_FACE target for the pod aim.

883	// CAMERA POD  --  the OV5640 RELOCATED off the board's back onto a 30cm FFC.
884	// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
885	// The -C's camera is a bare OV5640 module that PLUGS into a 24-pin 0.5mm DVP
886	// connector (schematic J2, "0.5-24pin-cam"). Unplugging it and running a 30cm
887	// FFC + coupler lets the camera live anywhere -- so it no longer has to ride the
888	// board. The board stays on the pedestal as the SCREEN; this pod carries the
889	// lens out over the bowl and aims it at the pet.
890	//
891	// WHAT THIS PART IS: a small open-back enclosure that captures the bare module.
892	// It is deliberately built to the WIDE-ANGLE / MAX envelope, because the exact
893	// module was not calipered -- generic 24-pin OV5640 modules run 12.5..14.0mm
894	// square with a wide-angle barrel up to 14mm dia standing up to ~11mm proud.
895	// Sized to the top of that range, a smaller real part just sits looser and is
896	// taken up by adhesive; sized to the middle, a big one would not fit at all.
897	//
898	// RETENTION, and why there are no clamp tabs: with a 14mm barrel on a 14mm PCB
899	// the barrel eats almost the whole front face, so there is no front bezel to
900	// grab -- only the four PCB CORNERS (corner radius 9.9 > barrel radius 7.0) show.
901	// A rigid tab would also have to guess the PCB thickness, which varies. So the
902	// scheme is the one the module actually wants: the PCB drops into the pocket
903	// (located in X/Y by the walls), its front face lands on the FRONT-STOP LEDGE
904	// (the front plate, which the barrel pokes through), and a bead of silicone from
905	// the open back holds it. Nothing rigid touches the barrel -- which matters if it
906	// is an AUTO-FOCUS module, whose barrel is a moving VCM element and jams if
907	// pressed. The lens tip stands proud of the front plate, so the pod never
908	// vignettes even a 120deg cone.

import sys,math
def bedcontact(path):
    tri=[]; area=0.0; foot_area=0.0
    xs=[];ys=[]
    verts=[]
    for line in open(path):
        s=line.split()
        if s and s[0]=='vertex':
            verts.append(tuple(map(float,s[1:4])))
            if len(verts)==3:
                (ax,ay,az),(bx,by,bz),(cx,cy,cz)=verts
                # triangle area
                ux,uy,uz=bx-ax,by-ay,bz-az; vx,vy,vz=cx-ax,cy-ay,cz-az
                cxp=uy*vz-uz*vy; cyp=uz*vx-ux*vz; czp=ux*vy-uy*vx

                    foot_area+=a
                verts=[]
    return foot_area
for p in sys.argv[1:]:

## The relocated camera

The OV5640 was unplugged from the board's 24-pin DVP connector and moved onto a
30 cm FFC so it can look at the bowl instead of riding the screen. Two printed
parts carry that:

* **`cam_pod`** — a small open-back enclosure for the bare module. Built to the
  **wide-angle MAX OV5640 envelope** (14 mm square PCB, 15 mm barrel aperture)
  because the exact module was not calipered; a smaller real part just sits
  looser and is taken up by a bead of silicone from the open back. Nothing rigid
  touches the barrel — it may be an auto-focus VCM element that jams if pressed.
  The lens tip stands proud of the front plate, so even a 120° cone never
  vignettes. Two Ø3.4 ears bolt it to the gantry.
* **the pedestal gantry** — not a separate file; it is part of
  `velapaw_pedestal_x1`. Two legs stand outboard of the screen cradle and two
  slender struts sweep up-and-forward over the top of the display to a tilted pad
  on the centreline. It rides the pedestal's existing four M3 bolts and adds **no
  new base-plate holes** — which is why the base plate did not have to change.

Validated in the assembly: the placed pod's aim ray lands on the pet-face target
(−25° down-and-forward), and the pod + gantry clear the board, hopper, drum,
bowl and chute (empty-intersection probes). The pedestal-plus-gantry is one
closed solid (`Simple: yes`, one volume).

**Caution — orientation before power.** A reversed FFC is fatal on first power:
board pin N mates camera pin 25−N, which puts a 1.5 V rail onto the camera's
ground and 2.8 V onto data lines. Before powering, buzz chassis ground to the
coupler's far contacts and confirm ground lands on the low-numbered (pin-2) end;
flip the cable if it shows at the pin-23/24 end.

**Caliper note.** If the real module is measured, tightening `POD_PCB` in the
`.scad` re-exports **both** `cam_pod` and `pedestal` — the gantry pad's hole
spacing tracks the pod outline (`EAR_X = POD_OUT/2 + POD_EAR_L/2`). Re-run the
two exports and the numbers above will shift slightly.

Now I can explain exactly what you're seeing. Reading lines 808–822:

- The file is in **`LAYOUT = "back"`**. In that layout the board's **own on-board camera** had to hang over the bowl, and since the screen and camera are on **opposite faces** of the board, aiming the camera down at the bowl forced the **screen to face the other way — behind the funnel** (line 818: *"screen faces BEHIND the funnel, owner stands behind"*). So right now you're looking at the **back of the board**; the screen is pointing away from you, toward the hopper side.

Here's the key point: **that backward-facing screen only existed because the camera was bolted to the board.** We just took the camera *off* the board and put it on its own gantry. So the constraint that forced the screen to face away is **gone** — the board is now purely a display and is free to face whoever's watching.

I've done enough geometry to give you a definitive answer, and it's a real fork worth your call before I rebuild anything. Here's what I found — and to be clear, **I have not touched the real `velapaw_feeder.scad`; all of this was on throwaway copies.**

## What I verified

Turning the screen to face you (the simple `rotate 180 → 0` flip) works *mechanically* — the flipped board clears the funnel, drum, and chute completely. But it collides with the **camera gantry I added earlier this session**, and not in a way I can just nudge around:

- **The booms** clip the board's top edge — fixable with a 6 mm lift (I found and validated the exact numbers: POD z 48→54, RIS_TOP 50→56; pod still aims dead-on at the pet, −23.9°).
- **The camera's line of sight is the real problem.** With the screen leaning *toward* you, the panel sits directly in the path the pod uses to look over the top of the board at the bowl — verified: the sightline passes straight through the screen body (z ≈ 7–44). Reaching the pod forward over the bowl doesn't escape it either, because a screen tilted toward you sprawls forward into that same space.

**Root cause:** the pod rides a gantry *behind* the screen and looks *over* it. That only works while the screen leans **away** from you (backward) — which is exactly why it's currently backward. The camera relocation freed the screen from *being* the camera, but my gantry re-introduced the same "screen must lean away" constraint. To face the screen to you, the camera has to stop looking over the screen.

The good news: the camera is on a 30 cm flex now, so it genuinely can go elsewhere. The question is where — and that reshapes the gantry, so I want your call.

## Where this landed

Your instinct was right — the screen **can** face you (it's a one-line flip). But chasing the camera around the pedestal hit a wall I can now state with certainty, having tested every variant:

**A user-facing screen sits directly between the machine and the pet.** The pet's face is low and forward (Y−142, z−52); the board occupies Y≈−104, z−13…+12. So *any* camera behind or above the screen — center, side (your pick), chin, top edge, even with the screen stood fully upright — has its line of sight cross the board body. I verified all of them blocked, and the block is always the same: the screen you want to see is in the way. The "side eye off the pedestal" can't win that, and it's not a tuning problem — it's the geometry.

The clean fix is to **stop making the camera peek past the screen** and decouple it — which is exactly what the 30 cm flex was for. A small eye **in front of the bowl, low, looking back at the pet** has clear air the whole way (verified clear). It's also the standard pet-feeder camera spot, and it can live on the **front edge of the `base_front` plate you're already printing** — no gantry, no new part, and the pedestal reverts to its simpler pre-gantry form.

So the choice below reshapes the earlier "side eye" decision with what I now know. I'll build whichever you pick without more back-and-forth.

54	holds the bare module and bolts to that gantry with 2× M3. Both ride
55	`order2_structure` because the pod↔gantry joint is an M3 clearance — machine
56	independent — so it does not need to share a print batch with anything. See
57	*The relocated camera* below. **Pod pocket is built to the wide-angle MAX OV5640
58	envelope; if the real module is calipered, tightening `POD_PCB` re-exports both
59	the pod and the pedestal (the pad hole spacing tracks the pod outline).**
60	
61	`support` is the **only** part with quantity 2 — the drum sits in an A-frame at
62	each end. The quantity is in the filename because it is the single easiest thing
63	to get wrong at the cart, and a missing A-frame means the machine cannot be
64	assembled at all.
65	
66	### Where the split line was drawn
67	
68	**Not by volume — by fits.** Every printed-to-printed fit in the model is inside
69	`order1_mechanism`: the rotor's running fit in the housing, its stub socket in
70	the idle plate, the hopper's saddle over the housing OD and its post scallops,
71	the A-frames' saddles over the plate ODs, the chute under the drum. Parts printed
72	in one batch share their systematic error — same machine, same flow calibration,
73	same spool — so they miss in the *same* direction. Split across two orders they
74	can miss in opposite directions, which is the worst corner every clearance was
75	sized against. Keeping the cluster together doesn't make the fits legal; it makes
76	them comfortable.
77	
78	Nothing in `order2_structure` touches the mechanism except through an M3 or M4
79	clearance hole, which does not care what machine its mate came off. That folder
80	can be printed on a different machine, in a different material, on a different
81	day, with no consequence.
82	
83	Both orders clear ¥50 of value at the bottom of the FDM range, so neither
84	voucher is wasted. **Do check the second shipping fee at checkout** — it is the
85	one cost that splitting adds, and it comes straight off the ¥50 gained.
86	
87	To order everything as a single job instead, upload both folders together — but
88	that redeems only one ¥50.
89	
90	## Deliberately NOT in this folder
91	
92	* **`board_cradle`** — the plain cradle. It is an *alternative* to
93	  `board_cradle_stand`, not an addition: the stand version contains the cradle.
94	  Ordering both wastes money and yields a part with nowhere to go. The stand
95	  version is the one the finished appliance uses.
96	* **`plate_servo`** — legacy MG90S mount, superseded by the stepper. Unused.
97	* **`stand`, `product`, `all`** — preview assemblies, not parts. `stand` is
98	  268 mm and exists only to show how the five stand pieces bolt together.
99	
100	## The board pocket
101	
102	`board_cradle_stand` holds the ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C in a pocket, and that
103	pocket is the **only fit in the model that had to be re-solved for FDM**. It is
104	also the only one where a bad outcome is not recoverable: everything else can be
105	reamed, filed or shimmed, but if this comes out tight the display does not seat
106	and the demo has no screen.
107	
108	The pocket is 95.11 × 63.67 mm — the largest feature in the model, so it sees
109	the full tolerance swing. At the old 0.6 mm/side (sized for MJF's ±0.3) an FDM
110	pocket printed to the tight end of ±0.5 would have left **0.1 mm**. It is now
111	**1.0 mm/side**, which leaves 0.5 mm at the same bad corner.
112	
113	Opening a pocket costs grip, because the retention lips start at the pocket wall
114	and retreat with it. `BM_LIP_W` went 2.0 → 2.8 to pay that back, restoring the
115	designed 1.8 mm of grip nominal / 0.8 mm with the board shoved fully to one side.
116	Two supporting changes came with it: the pocket wall went 2.4 → 2.8 nominal so
117	the *printed* wall stays at 1.8 mm (1.3 mm worst case) instead of dropping under
118	JLCPCB's 1.2 mm FDM minimum, and the lip's retaining face went 1.2 → 1.6 mm to
119	get off that minimum, since it is the face that takes the whole pull-out load.
120	
121	Verified by solid-geometry probe, not by arithmetic alone:
122	
123	| Probe | Expected | Result |
124	|---|---|---|
125	| case seats in pocket, nominal | empty intersection | clear |
126	| case seats with pocket 0.3 mm undersize (MJF worst case) | empty | clear |
127	| case seats with pocket 0.5 mm undersize (**FDM worst case**) | empty | clear |
128	| far lip still over the board, board shoved 1.0 mm away | **non**-empty | material present |
129	| enlarged cradle vs. every neighbour in the assembly | 13 separate bodies | 13 |
130	
131	Net cost: the part grew 0.8 mm in each outer dimension and 3 cm³ in volume.
132	Nothing is competing for that space.
133	
134	## The relocated camera
135	
136	The OV5640 was unplugged from the board's 24-pin DVP connector and moved onto a
137	30 cm FFC so it can look at the bowl instead of riding the screen. Two printed
138	parts carry that:
139	
140	* **`cam_pod`** — a small open-back enclosure for the bare module. Built to the
141	  **wide-angle MAX OV5640 envelope** (14 mm square PCB, 15 mm barrel aperture)
142	  because the exact module was not calipered; a smaller real part just sits
143	  looser and is taken up by a bead of silicone from the open back. Nothing rigid
144	  touches the barrel — it may be an auto-focus VCM element that jams if pressed.
145	  The lens tip stands proud of the front plate, so even a 120° cone never
146	  vignettes. Two Ø3.4 ears bolt it to the gantry.
147	* **the pedestal gantry** — not a separate file; it is part of
148	  `velapaw_pedestal_x1`. Two legs stand outboard of the screen cradle and two
149	  slender struts sweep up-and-forward over the top of the display to a tilted pad
150	  on the centreline. It rides the pedestal's existing four M3 bolts and adds **no
151	  new base-plate holes** — which is why the base plate did not have to change.
152	
153	Validated in the assembly: the placed pod's aim ray lands on the pet-face target
154	(−25° down-and-forward), and the pod + gantry clear the board, hopper, drum,
155	bowl and chute (empty-intersection probes). The pedestal-plus-gantry is one
156	closed solid (`Simple: yes`, one volume).
157	
158	**Caution — orientation before power.** A reversed FFC is fatal on first power:
159	board pin N mates camera pin 25−N, which puts a 1.5 V rail onto the camera's
160	ground and 2.8 V onto data lines. Before powering, buzz chassis ground to the
161	coupler's far contacts and confirm ground lands on the low-numbered (pin-2) end;
162	flip the cable if it shows at the pin-23/24 end.
163	
164	**Caliper note.** If the real module is measured, tightening `POD_PCB` in the
165	`.scad` re-exports **both** `cam_pod` and `pedestal` — the gantry pad's hole
166	spacing tracks the pod outline (`EAR_X = POD_OUT/2 + POD_EAR_L/2`). Re-run the
167	two exports and the numbers above will shift slightly.
168	
169	## Pre-upload verification (measured on THESE files, not on the source)
170	
171	Run `verify_stl.py` and `bedcontact.py` against **each order folder** to
172	reproduce. Both folders were re-verified after the split — the checks below are
173	the union of the two runs, and nothing changed in the move.
174	
175	**Watertight — all 12 pass all four conditions.** "Watertight" is four separate
176	things, and a mesh can pass the naive check and still be rejected. The two
177	order2 files changed by the camera relocation (`pedestal`, `cam_pod`) were
178	re-verified by CGAL (`Simple: yes`, one closed volume each) and z=0 seating:
179	
180	| Condition | Result |
181	|---|---|
182	| every edge shared by exactly 2 triangles (no holes/open edges) | 0 open edges |
183	| consistent winding — each directed edge used once | 0 bad |
184	| signed volume > 0 (normals point **out**, not in) | all positive |
185	| exactly 1 connected component per file | all 1 |
186	| zero-area/degenerate triangles | 0 |
187	
188	**Orientation — all 12 sit on z = 0.000 on a real FACE**, not an edge or a
189	vertex. First-layer contact area, which is the check that actually matters:
190	
191	| Part | bed contact | height |
192	|---|---|---|
193	| base_front | 28738 mm² (100% of footprint) | 15 |
194	| base_back | 14835 mm² (98%) | 15 |
195	| plate_idle | 4028 mm² (78%) | 11 |
196	| plate_stepper | 3904 mm² (75%) | 4 |
197	| support | 4652 mm² (31%) | 16 |
198	| rotor | 549 mm² (19%) | 38 |
199	| cam_pod | 208 mm² (front plate, 54%) | 8 |
200	| housing | 629 mm² (15%) | 39.2 |
201	| hopper | 886 mm² (10%) | 80.7 |
202	| chute | 430 mm² (9%) | 92.5 |
203	| pedestal | 709 mm² | 185 |
204	| board_cradle_stand | 388 mm² (5%) | 81.0 |
205	
206	The **pedestal is now 185 mm tall** (was 102) — the camera gantry cantilevers
207	forward at the top to carry the pod out over the screen. On FDM that overhang
208	wants "support on build plate only" like the rails already did; on MJF it is a
209	non-issue. It still lands on the same 709 mm² of foot pads, on z=0.
210	
211	The low-ratio parts are tall and open by design; every one still lands on a flat
212	face. **On MJF none of this is binding** — it is a powder bed, JLC nest the parts
213	themselves, and there is no bed adhesion to lose. The poses are submitted correct
214	anyway because they make JLC's preview legible and they are what proves the set
215	could be made on a filament machine if it ever has to be.
216	
217	## Material volume — read this before ordering
218	
219	**651 cm³ total, ~0.66 kg of PA12** (includes support ×2). MJF is quoted mostly
220	by volume, so this is the number that sets the price. (Was 593 before the camera
221	relocation, which added the pedestal gantry +55.5 cm³ and the pod +2.2 cm³.)
222	
223	Nearly half of it is still the base plate:
224	
225	| | cm³ | share |
226	|---|---|---|
227	| base_front | 178.9 | 27% |
228	| base_back | 94.1 | 14% |
229	| **base plate subtotal** | **273.0** | **42%** |
230	| everything else (10 parts, 11 pieces) | 378.5 | 58% |
231	
232	By order: `order1_mechanism` 229 cm³ (35%), `order2_structure` 423 cm³ (65%).
233	The structure order is the expensive one, and it now carries the camera as well:
234	base plate 273, pedestal-with-gantry 102, board cradle 45, pod 2.
235	
236	That is a 5 mm solid floor over 164 × 176 and 164 × 92 mm.
237	
238	**DECIDED (2026-07-25): the base plate is being printed.** Substituting a cut
239	sheet of MDF or acrylic was considered and rejected, so the full base plate
240	stands (273 cm³ of the 651) and the two-order split holds as described above. Do
241	not re-open this at the cart.
242	
243	If volume ever does have to come out of it, the thing to know is that the floor
244	thickness is **not** a free parameter: the M3 × 12 countersunk tower screws are
245	dimensioned around exactly 5 mm (csk sinks 1.4, screw protrudes 7 into a 9 mm
246	flange). Thinning the floor means re-solving the screw stack. Pocketing or
247	ribbing the floor *between* the tower feet and the bowl ring is the change that
248	saves volume without touching the fastener scheme.
249	
250	## Sanity checks to run in JLC's uploader
251	
252	1. **Scale.** `velapaw_base_front_x1` must read ~**164 × 176 × 15 mm**. STL
253	   carries no units; if the viewer shows inches or centimetres the whole order
254	   is wrong by a constant factor and every part will be useless.
255	2. **Watertight / manifold.** All eleven pass locally — CGAL reports
256	   `Simple: yes`, one closed volume, zero bad edges. If JLC's checker disagrees,
257	   suspect the upload, not the geometry.
258	3. **No trapped powder.** No part has an internal void, so there is nothing for
259	   un-sintered powder to be sealed inside. The deepest blind holes are the four
260	   ⌀1.7 × 12 pilots down the cradle posts, which are vestigial on the -C board
261	   (see `BM_SCREW_D` in the .scad) — they may be ignored or filled.
262	
263	## Fasteners — buy separately, NOT printed
264	
265	| Item | Qty | Where |
266	|---|---|---|
267	| M3 × 12 countersunk | 12 | towers → base plate (2 per foot, 6 feet) |
268	| M3 × 22 socket cap | 2 | base_front → base_back splice |
269	| M3 (plates → housing) | 8 | end plates onto the drum |
270	| M4 | 2 | 28BYJ-48 stepper flange |
271	| M3 × 8 self-tapping | 2 | camera pod → gantry pad (through Ø3.4 ears into Ø2.6 pilots) |
272	
273	## After delivery
274	
275	The 28BYJ-48 D-shaft socket in the rotor is the one fit deliberately held
276	tighter than the MJF clearance rule, because it is the only joint transmitting
277	torque and slop there means mis-dosing. At the tight end of the tolerance it
278	will need a 5 mm drill run through by hand and a light file on the two flats.
279	Budget 30 seconds for it; it is intentional, not a defect.

140	## The relocated camera
141	
142	The OV5640 was unplugged from the board's 24-pin DVP connector and moved onto a
143	30 cm FFC so it can look at the bowl instead of riding the screen. **The screen
144	now faces the owner** (the board is un-rotated on its wedge), which means a
145	camera behind or above the bowl would have to shoot *through* the display — so
146	the camera is decoupled onto its own front post. Two printed parts carry it:
147	
148	* **`cam_pod`** — a small open-back enclosure for the bare module. Built to the
149	  **wide-angle MAX OV5640 envelope** (14 mm square PCB, 15 mm barrel aperture)
150	  because the exact module was not calipered; a smaller real part just sits
151	  looser and is taken up by a bead of silicone from the open back. Nothing rigid
152	  touches the barrel — it may be an auto-focus VCM element that jams if pressed.
153	  The lens tip stands proud of the front plate, so even a 120° cone never
154	  vignettes. Two Ø3.4 ears bolt it to the mast pad.
155	* **`cam_mast`** — a slim post (29 × 35 × 89 mm, ~20 cm³) that bolts to
156	  `base_front` at the front-right corner with **2× M3**, standing outside the
157	  bowl locating ring (82 mm from centre). It rises above the front bowl rim and
158	  its top is a tilted pad, built in the pod's own frame, that carries the pod's
159	  two ears. It is a **separate bolt-on part**, so the pedestal reverted to its
160	  plain 46 cm³ form.
161	
162	The camera aim is now **compound** — the eye is off-axis at X = +60, so the pod
163	swings about Z (yaw 59.0°) and tilts about X (pitch 83.5°) to lay its lens onto
164	the pet-face target. Validated in the assembly by CGAL: pod, mast and the aim
165	sightline each clear the board, hopper, drum, bowl and chute (empty
166	intersections), and `cam_mast` is one closed solid (`Simple: yes`, one volume).

171	coupler's far contacts and confirm ground lands on the low-numbered (pin-2) end;
