1	# VelaPaw — feeder hardware
2	
3	Gravity hopper → **paddle rotor** → chute → bowl, driven by one hobby servo on GPIO43.
4	
5	## Why a rotor and not a flap
6	
7	A flap's dose depends on how long it stays open **and** how full the hopper is — the same 800 ms drops noticeably more food when the hopper is heavy. A rotor pocket holds a fixed volume, so the dose depends only on how many pockets you index. Since the product claim is *per-pet portion control*, a mechanism that drifts as the hopper empties would quietly undermine it.
8	
9	The rotor is driven by a **28BYJ-48 stepper** (via a ULN2003 board), which rotates **continuously in one direction** — so pockets ratchet inlet→outlet and per-pocket dosing is exact:
10	
11	```
12	grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET
13	```
14	
15	> **Why a stepper, not a servo.** An MG90S servo can only *oscillate*, and with the inlet and outlet 180° apart a zero-net-rotation wobble can never carry a pocket across — it dispenses the initial charge then dead-heads. The stepper's continuous spin is what makes the rotary valve actually work, and it makes the portion-control claim literally true. (The geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque, which resists kibble jams.)
16	
17	## Bill of materials
18	
19	| Item | Notes |
20	|---|---|
21	| **28BYJ-48 stepper + ULN2003 driver** (5 V bundle) | The **5 V** version — runs off the same 5 V supply below. Get the motor+driver bundle. |
22	| **5 V supply, ≥2 A** | Powers the ULN2003/motor. Common **ground** with the ESP32; never tie the 5 V rails together. |
23	| Female–female jumpers | 4 signal lines (IN1–IN4) + 5 V + GND to the ULN2003. |
24	| PLA / PETG (or JLC nylon) | PLA is fine for dry kibble; PETG/nylon if you want to wash the parts. |
25	
26	The **ULN2003 board is the driver** — no separate PWM chip; the ESP32-S3 just toggles 4 GPIOs through the half-step sequence. (No servo → the 470 µF servo-inrush cap is no longer needed.)
27	
28	## Wiring
29	
30	```
31	  ESP32-S3 (3.3 V logic)            ULN2003 driver board          28BYJ-48
32	    GPIO12 ─────────────────────────> IN1
33	    GPIO13 ─────────────────────────> IN2                         (5-pin
34	    GPIO15 ─────────────────────────> IN3            motor  ────►  connector)
35	    GPIO16 ─────────────────────────> IN4
36	                                      +   ◄── 5 V PSU +
37	                                      −   ◄──┬─ 5 V PSU −
38	  board GND ───────────────────────────────┘   ← COMMON GROUND, mandatory
39	```
40	
41	- **GPIO12/13/15/16** are the ES8311 audio-codec lines; VelaPaw uses no audio, so they're free (all ESP32→codec directions, safe to drive). Change them in the board file (`STEP_IN1..4`) if you ever add audio.
42	- **Power the ULN2003 from the separate 5 V supply, not the board**, and share **ground only**. The 28BYJ-48 draws ~240 mA/phase — fine for a 2 A supply.
43	- The ULN2003's on-board LEDs show the coil sequence — handy for confirming it's stepping.
44	
45	## Printing
46	
47	All parts print without supports. PLA/PETG, 0.2 mm layers, 3 perimeters.
48	
49	```bash
50	openscad -D 'part="rotor"'       -o rotor.stl       velapaw_feeder.scad
51	openscad -D 'part="housing"'     -o housing.stl     velapaw_feeder.scad
52	openscad -D 'part="plate_servo"' -o plate_servo.stl velapaw_feeder.scad
53	openscad -D 'part="plate_idle"'  -o plate_idle.stl  velapaw_feeder.scad
54	openscad -D 'part="hopper"'      -o hopper.stl      velapaw_feeder.scad
55	openscad -D 'part="board_cradle"' -o board_cradle.stl velapaw_feeder.scad
56	```
57	
58	Open the file with no `-D` to preview the assembly.
59	
60	## Board cradle (mounting the ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C)
61	
62	`board_cradle` holds the Waveshare board **screen-up** so the owner reads the
63	display, while the **camera** (dead-centre of the board's back) looks **straight
64	down through a window at the bowl**. The board drops into the tray and is fixed
65	with four **M2.5** screws through its corner mounting holes into the posts; the
66	bottom GPIO header (and the servo signal wire to GPIO43) exits through the header
67	slot.
68	
69	Dimensions are taken from the Waveshare -C outline drawing (95.11 × 63.67 × 14.1 mm,
70	corner R7.3, mounting holes 72.00 × 48.50 mm apart, camera centred). **Two values
71	are not on the drawing and are assumed — verify on the real board before printing:**
72	`BM_SCREW_D` (mounting-hole/screw size, assumed M2.5) and `BM_CAM_WIN` (camera
73	lens-barrel diameter, assumed Ø14). Both are near the bottom of the `.scad`.
74	
75	> ### Stepper mechanical parts — done (verify two dimensions)
76	> The drive end is now built for the **28BYJ-48**: print **`plate_stepper`** (its
77	> Ø28 body clears the central bore; it bolts on through the two 35 mm flange
78	> holes) — *not* `plate_servo`, which is kept only as legacy reference. The
79	> **rotor** now has a **5 mm double-D socket** in its driven face that presses
80	> straight onto the stepper shaft (no horn/spline). Body Ø is confirmed 28 mm;
81	> two values are nominal — **caliper before printing** and adjust at the top of
82	> the `.scad`: `STEP_SHAFT_FLAT` (shaft width across the flats) and
83	> `STEP_SHAFT_LEN` (shaft length). `housing`, `plate_idle`, `hopper` and
84	> `board_cradle` are unchanged.
85	
86	## Assembly (servo-era steps — the drive end changes with the stepper, see above)
87	
88	1. ~~Screw the servo into `plate_servo`~~ → mount the **28BYJ-48** to its new plate (flange screws).
89	2. ~~Screw the round horn into the rotor hub~~ → press the rotor's **D-socket** onto the stepper shaft.
90	3. Drop the rotor into the `housing` bore.
91	4. Fit `plate_idle` on the far end — its boss is the rotor's stub axle.
92	5. Bolt both plates to the housing (4 × M3).
93	6. Plug the `hopper` spigot into the inlet; put a bowl under the outlet.
94	
95	## Calibration — do this once
96	
97	1. Fill the hopper.
98	2. Dispense a single pocket.
99	3. Weigh what lands in the bowl.
100	4. Put that number in `GRAMS_PER_POCKET` in `board/esp32s3_st7789.c` and rebuild.
101	
102	Portions are then correct at any hopper level, for the life of the machine. If you want a different dose granularity, change `WIDTH` in the `.scad` (pocket volume scales linearly with it) and re-calibrate.
103	
104	`POCKETS` in the `.scad` must always equal `ROTOR_POCKETS` in the board file.
105

1 English | 中文 2 3 # VelaPaw — Engineering Deep-Dive 4 5 Technical notes on how VelaPaw is built: the on-device AI pipeline, the depth of 6 openVela use, the hardest problems solved, and the performance engineering. This 7 is the companion to the [README](../README.md) for readers who want the details. 8 9 --- 10 11 ## 1. System at a glance 12 13 Everything runs on a single **ESP32-S3** (Xtensa LX7, 8 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash) 14 under **openVela / NuttX**, with an **LVGL** touchscreen UI. There is no 15 companion phone, no cloud, and no network dependency — capture, inference, 16 scheduling, timekeeping and dispensing are all local. 17 18 **Flash layout (16 MB)** 19 20 | Offset | Contents | Size | Note | 21 |---|---|---|---| 22 | `0x000000` | Firmware (`nuttx.bin`) | ~750 KB | openVela + app + LVGL | 23 | `0x600000` | Identity model (`velapaw.tflite`) | 1.44 MB | flash-loaded to PSRAM at boot | 24 | `0x760000` | Body-condition model (`bcs.tflite`) | 626 KB | flash-loaded to PSRAM at boot | 25 | `0x800000` | Enrolled pets (magic `VPAW`) | 8 KB | names, schedules, face embeddings | 26 | `0x810000` | Pet photos (magic `VICN`) | 32 KB | card thumbnails | 27 28 The two neural networks are **too large to memory-map** — the DROM0 MMU window 29 saturates well before a 1.4 MB `const` array maps — so they are flashed as raw 30 blobs and read into PSRAM buffers at boot via the NuttX software `spi_flash_read` 31 path. Because flash reads suspend the CPU cache, that read runs on a short-lived 32 thread whose stack is a `.bss` (internal-SRAM) buffer. 33 34 --- 35 36 ## 2. The recognition pipeline 37 38 ``` 39 camera frame ─► embed (TFLM INT8, background worker) ─► cosine match vs enrolled 40 │ 41 pet id + score + margin 42 │ 43 schedule gate: is a meal of THIS pet 44 due today and not yet eaten? 45 │yes │no 46 dispense N g show next meal 47 │ 48 log history · trends · body-condition 49 ``` 50 51 **Open-set, not closed-set.** Recognition is metric learning, not an N-way 52 classifier: the model maps a 128×128 frame to an L2-normalized 128-D embedding, 53 enrollment stores the averaged embedding of a few photos, and matching is cosine 54 similarity against the enrolled set. The practical payoff is that **adding a pet 55 requires no retraining** — enrollment is a runtime operation, and the accepted/ 56 rejected decision is a tunable threshold. (A consequence worth knowing: rejecting 57 arbitrary non-pet objects is inherently hard for a generic feature extractor, so 58 enrollment quality — tight, well-lit face shots — is the dominant lever on 59 false-accepts.) 60 61 **Inference is off the UI thread.** The ~1.3 s `Invoke()` runs on a dedicated 62 worker thread; the LVGL loop hands it a frame and keeps rendering, so touch and 63 the camera preview stay live during inference. Recognition is also **on-demand** 64 (it runs when a pet is at the bowl, not continuously) to bound the workload. 65 66 --- 67 68 ## 3. Depth of openVela use 69 70 VelaPaw is not a thin app on top of a BSP — it exercises openVela across the 71 stack: 72 73 - **`apps/mlearning/tflite-micro`** is the AI runtime. The app links it directly 74 (`backend_tflm.cc`) and runs two independent `MicroInterpreter`s (identity + 75 body-condition) with PSRAM tensor arenas. 76 - **LVGL** (openVela graphics) drives the four-tab touch UI. 77 - **Custom board bring-up** (`board/esp32s3_st7789.c`) drives, from scratch on 78 the ESP32-S3 peripherals: 79 - the **ST7796 display** over hardware SPI2 + GDMA; 80 - the **OV5640 camera** via the **LCD_CAM** peripheral with a GDMA receive 81 channel (configured over SCCB/I²C); 82 - the **PCF85063 RTC** over I²C (raw register access — no `CONFIG_RTC`, which 83 keeps the USB-CDC console alive); 84 - the **feeder servo** over an **LEDC/PWM** channel. 85 - **Auto-start** (`board/esp32s3_appinit.c`) launches the app from 86 `board_app_initialize()` — NSH calls it via `boardctl(BOARDIOC_INIT)` after 87 `esp32s3_bringup()` has registered the LCD/touch/camera — so the device boots 88 straight into its UI while keeping the shell available for debugging. 89 90 --- 91 92 ## 4. The hardest problem: hardware-SPI display 93 94 This is the standout piece of hardware debugging in the project. 95 96 **Symptom.** Over hardware SPI, a *full-screen* write rendered, but *any partial 97 window* (`CASET`/`RASET` to a sub-rectangle + `RAMWR`) never appeared — while the 98 identical byte sequence over a bit-banged GPIO path worked perfectly. It survived 99 ~60 build cycles of software and config changes (framebuffer mirroring, DMA on/ 100 off, software CS, PSRAM-coherency fixes, pin-routing forcing). 101 102 **Method — measure, don't guess.** With a logic analyzer (sigrok/PulseView on an 103 FX2 clone), the SPI pins can't be probed directly — they're not on the header — 104 so the board firmware **mirrors** `FSPID_OUT`/`FSPICLK_OUT` onto spare header 105 GPIOs via the GPIO matrix, plus a trigger marker. A decisive first step was a 106 **ground-truth test**: drive four known square waves on the probe pins and refuse 107 to trust any capture until they read clean. That immediately exposed a wiring/ 108 grounding problem that had been producing garbage — and only *then* did the real 109 capture become trustworthy. 110 111 **Finding.** The decoded capture showed the ESP32 emitting a **byte-perfect** 112 `CASET 00 28 00 8B / RASET 00 28 00 8B / RAMWR / pixels` stream — correct 113 commands, correct DC alignment, exactly 8 clean clock edges per byte, zero 114 glitches. The peripheral was innocent all along. 115 116 **Root cause.** The panel's **chip-select is hardwired low**, so it can never 117 re-synchronize its bit counter on a CS edge — it counts clock edges forever. The 118 firmware bit-banged the panel init and *then* handed the pads to the SPI 119 peripheral; that pad handover glitches the clock by a single edge, and from that 120 instant the panel is off by one bit. Every subsequent command decodes as garbage, 121 `RAMWR` is never recognized, no pixels reach GRAM, and the screen simply keeps 122 showing whatever bit-bang last painted — which looked exactly like "hardware SPI 123 renders nothing." 124 125 **Fix.** Give the pads to the SPI peripheral **first**, then **hardware-reset the 126 panel** (a software reset can't work — it would itself be misread), then run the 127 entire init over SPI. Once the panel is re-synced under SPI ownership, partial 128 windows render correctly. 129 130 **Payoff.** With the path proven, the display was moved off bit-banging entirely 131 and onto hardware SPI (see §5). A bug that looked like a dead end became a 132 performance win. 133 134 --- 135 136 ## 5. Performance engineering 137 138 **ESP-NN on the LX7 (≈5× inference speed-up).** The identity model is mostly 139 depthwise convolution, which runs slowly on the TFLite-Micro *reference* kernels 140 (~6.75 s / inference). Wiring in the **ESP-NN** SIMD kernels for the Xtensa LX7 141 brings it to **~1.3 s**. The subtle part was that the ESP-NN kernel set has to be 142 dropped into the tflite-micro kernel directory and the matching *reference* 143 kernels filtered out to avoid duplicate symbols; and a class of "crash on first 144 conv" turned out to be **stale incremental builds**, not a kernel bug — a clean 145 build runs stably. 146 147 **Hardware SPI + DMA display (≈4× UI repaint speed-up).** Once the SPI path was 148 correct (§4), the display went from bit-banging every pixel (CPU toggling GPIOs) 149 to the hardware SPI2 peripheral at **40 MHz with GDMA**. A full 480×320 repaint 150 dropped from **~246 ms to ~61 ms**. Two details mattered: pixel rows are bounced 151 through an internal-SRAM buffer because SPI DMA can't read PSRAM cache-coherently, 152 and the address-window setup was batched from 11 SPI calls down to 5 (LVGL sets a 153 window on every `putarea`). 154 155 --- 156 157 ## 6. Build & reproducibility notes 158 159 A few non-obvious constraints, recorded so the build is reproducible: 160 161 - **App/library define parity.** The app and the prebuilt `tflite-micro` library 162 share headers, so header-visible defines must match exactly. In particular 163 `TF_LITE_STATIC_MEMORY` changes the layout of `TfLiteTensor` — defining it on 164 only one side lets `AllocateTensors` pass but makes the first `Invoke` write 165 through a mis-offset pointer and wedge the SoC. The Makefile mirrors the 166 library's define set exactly. 167 - **`-fno-threadsafe-statics`** is required on the C++ flags: without it the first 168 function-local static in TFLM init deadlocks in `__cxa_guard_acquire` on this 169 libsupc++ build (a silent hang, not a crash). 170 - **Config changes re-clone esp-hal**, which reverts a spinlock initializer patch; 171 the first build after any defconfig change may need the patch re-applied. 172 173 ### ESP-NN acceleration — a public-repo change, provided as a fork/PR 174 175 The ~1.3 s inference figure requires the **ESP-NN** SIMD kernels, and that 176 integration modifies a **public** openVela repo (`apps/mlearning/tflite-micro`). 177 Per the contest rules — *public-repo changes are submitted as a fork-and-PR to 178 `dev-ai-contest-2026`, not committed into the team repo* — the ESP-NN work is 179 delivered as a fork/PR rather than vendored here. **Out of the box, this team 180 repo builds and runs with the reference kernels (~6.75 s); applying the ESP-NN 181 fork brings it to ~1.3 s.** 182 183 The integration consists of three parts: 184 185 1. **The esp-nn library** (Espressif's Apache-2.0 SIMD kernels for the Xtensa 186 LX7) added at `apps/mlearning/esp-nn/`. 187 2. **Kernel wrappers** (`conv`, `depthwise_conv`, `fully_connected`, `pooling`, 188 `add`, `mul`, `softmax`) dropped into 189 `apps/mlearning/tflite-micro/tflite-micro/tensorflow/lite/micro/kernels/esp_nn/`. 190 3. **A Makefile block** in `apps/mlearning/tflite-micro/Makefile` that compiles 191 the esp-nn sources with `-DESP_NN=1 -DCONFIG_NN_OPTIMIZED -mlongcalls`, adds 192 its include dirs, and **filters out the matching reference kernels** so there 193 are no duplicate symbols. 194 195 The exact wrappers, the Makefile block, and a step-by-step reproduction recipe 196 are provided as reference material in [`docs/esp-nn/`](esp-nn/). 197 198 > **PR:** _``_ 199 200 Two gotchas found during the integration: the esp-nn assembly sources 201 (`*esp32s3.c`) are excluded (the opt-C path is used); and an early "crash on the 202 first conv" was traced to **stale incremental builds**, not a kernel fault — a 203 clean rebuild runs stably. 204 205 --- 206 207 ## 7. Off-device: model training 208 209 The two INT8 models are trained off-device with the pipeline in [`host/`](../host/) 210 (TensorFlow/Keras). The identity model is a MobileNetV3-Small backbone with a 211 spatial-attention **TSFM** module and an ArcFace metric-learning head; it is 212 exported via INT8 post-training quantization to a `.tflite` whose ops are all 213 TFLM builtins. The body-condition model is a compact 3-class CNN trained the same 214 way. See [`docs/BENCHMARK_AB.md`](BENCHMARK_AB.md) for the fast-vs-accurate model 215 comparison. 216 217 --- 218 219 *This document reflects the engineering as built and verified on real ESP32-S3 220 hardware.* 221

input.new_string:
## Camera relocation (OV5640 on a 30 cm FFC)

The OV5640 plugs into the board's 24-pin 0.5 mm DVP connector (schematic **J2**,
"0.5-24pin-cam"). Unplugging it and running a **30 cm FFC + a 1:1 coupler** lets
the camera live on its own mount instead of riding the board, so the screen can
face the owner while the lens watches the bowl. The camera sits in **`cam_pod`**
(open-back OV5640 enclosure) carried by **`cam_mast`** — a two-leg yoke that
straddles the chute and holds the pod just in front of the drum, aimed steeply
down-and-forward at the pet (the sightline passes *under* the owner-facing
screen's bottom edge). `cam_mast` bolts to `base_front` with 2× M3.

> **⚠️ A reversed FFC is FATAL on first power-on** — board pin *N* would meet
> camera pin *25−N*, dead-shorting a power rail into a data/ground pin. **Verify
> orientation with a meter before powering.** Verified-good chain (2026-07-30):
>
> ```
> camera pin 1 → pigtail "1" → coupler P1.1 (left) → P2.1 (left)
>              → 30 cm cable pin-1 (dotted edge) → J2 pin 1 (BOTTOM end of J2)
> ```
>
> Key facts for this module: the **coupler is a straight 1:1 extender** (silk
> `1`-left / `24`-right on both ports), **J2 pin 1 = the bottom end** (board silk
> prints `24` at the top), and the camera's **grounds are not bonded internally**
> — so you can't confirm orientation by probing *through* the camera; trust the
> silkscreen `1`/`24` marks and bare-copper (`000.x`) continuity only. Keep the
> ~30 cm run in a small **service loop** at the yoke foot for strain relief, and
> route it away from the stepper leads to keep noise off the DVP clock/data lines.

## Assembly

1. Mount the **28BYJ-48** to `plate_stepper` (flange screws).
2. Press the rotor's **D-socket** onto the stepper shaft.
3. Drop the rotor into the `housing` bore.

# Session State — "Resume From Here"

Last updated: 2026-07-30. Drop-in context so any new session (or a returning one) can continue with zero re-discovery.

## TL;DR status

- **Project:** VelaPaw — multi-pet recognition smart feeder, on-device AI (contest2026_043_CircuitForge). Track: AI Hardware Product Innovation.
- **Board:** Waveshare **ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C** (ESP32-S3, 8 MB PSRAM, 16 MB flash, ST7796 320×480 touch LCD, OV5640 camera, PCF85063 RTC).
- **Source checkout:** `D:\openVela` (NOT C:). Full openVela tree synced. Session anchor cwd is `C:\Users\VICTUS\openVela` (holds only `.claude`); real work is on D:.
- **Where it stands: running on real hardware.** On-device recognition (open-set metric learning, INT8), body-condition scoring, recognition-gated 3-meals/day scheduling, portion + daily-limit control, feeding history/trends with appetite-drop alerts, hardware RTC timekeeping, full pet lifecycle with persistent flash storage + photos, auto-start into the UI, and a hardware-SPI + DMA display. The **28BYJ-48 stepper feeder** turns, and the **OV5640 is relocated onto a 30 cm FFC** and confirmed working.
- **Next:** final mechanical assembly (mount the stepper dispenser + relocated camera into the printed enclosure). Reconcile the one code/wiring nit below (`STEP_IN4`).

## What works on hardware today

- **Recognition:** MobileNetV3-Small + TSFM attention → L2-normalized 128-D embedding; cosine match vs enrolled pets; match threshold 0.45. ESP-NN kernels bring inference to **~1.3 s** (vs ~6.75 s reference). Inference runs on a **background worker thread** so the LVGL UI stays live.
- **Body condition:** compact 3-class INT8 CNN (under/ideal/over).
- **Feeding:** recognition-gated — dispense only when *this* pet is recognized at the bowl **and** one of *its* meals is due & unfed today. Portions in grams via the paddle-rotor; hard daily cap.
- **Scheduling / clock:** meal times gated by the **PCF85063 RTC** driven directly over I²C (raw register access).
- **UI:** LVGL four-tab touch UI (Enroll · Recognize · My Pets · Trends). Trends tab has colored intake bars + appetite line chart + BCS gauge. EN/中文 bilingual string table with a live language toggle (CJK font blob pending).
- **Display:** ST7796 over hardware **SPI2 @ 40 MHz + GDMA** (full 480×320 repaint ~61 ms).
- **Persistence:** enrolled pets/schedules/embeddings at flash `0x800000`; pet photos at `0x810000`.

## Hardware wiring — the facts that bite

- **Console is on the USB-Serial/JTAG port**, NOT UART0. This is why UART0 pins are free for other use.
- **Feeder = 28BYJ-48 stepper via ULN2003**, four GPIOs: IN1/IN2/IN3 = GPIO12/13/15 (ES8311 audio lines, unused), **IN4 = GPIO43** (U0TXD, free because console is USB-Serial/JTAG).
  - **Use GPIO43, NOT GPIO44.** GPIO44 (U0RXD) is clamped and won't drive the coil cleanly — this was the "buzzes but won't turn" symptom during bring-up (it was the pin, not the coil order).
  - ⚠️ **Code nit to reconcile:** `board/esp32s3_st7789.c` currently defines `#define STEP_IN4 16` (an audio line) with an 8-step half-step table. The working wiring is **GPIO43**. Update `STEP_IN4` to `43` (and confirm the drive table) so the firmware matches the physical build.
- **Camera OV5640 relocated onto a 30 cm FFC + 1:1 coupler** into the `cam_mast` yoke in front of the bowl (see `hardware/README.md`). **A reversed FFC is FATAL on power-on** — orientation is meter-verified. Verified chain: camera pin 1 → pigtail "1" → coupler P1.1(left) → P2.1(left) → 30 cm cable pin-1(dotted) → **J2 pin 1 = bottom end**. The camera's grounds are NOT bonded internally, so you can't verify orientation by probing *through* it — trust silk `1`/`24` marks + bare-copper continuity only.

## Critical "do not" list (each has cost us real time)

- **Never enable `CONFIG_RTC`** — it kills the USB-CDC console. The PCF85063 is driven directly over I²C instead.
- **Never raw-write `spi_flash` at offset `0x818000`** — it wedges the SoC.
- **`-fno-threadsafe-statics` is mandatory** on the C++ flags — without it the first function-local static in TFLM init deadlocks in `__cxa_guard_acquire` (silent hang, THE blue-screen cause).
- **App/library define parity** — the app and prebuilt `tflite-micro` share headers; `TF_LITE_STATIC_MEMORY` etc. must match on both sides or the first `Invoke` wedges the SoC. The app Makefile mirrors the library's `-D` set exactly (incl. `MicroPrintf`).
- Large models are **flash-loaded to PSRAM at boot** (too big to memory-map); the flash read runs on a short-lived thread with a `.bss` stack because flash reads suspend the cache.

## Build & run (real hardware)

```bash
# board files into the ESP32-S3 board tree, then build from the openVela root
BOARD=nuttx/boards/xtensa/esp32s3/esp32s3-devkit
cp contest2026_043_CircuitForge/board/esp32s3_st7789.c  $BOARD/src/
cp contest2026_043_CircuitForge/board/esp32s3_appinit.c $BOARD/src/
cp contest2026_043_CircuitForge/board/configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig \
   $BOARD/configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig
./build.sh esp32s3-devkit:waveshare_lcd -j8

# flash firmware + the two on-device models
esptool --chip esp32s3 --port <PORT> write-flash \
  0x0      nuttx/nuttx.bin \
  0x600000 contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/infer/model/velapaw.tflite \
  0x760000 contest2026_043_CircuitForge/app/velapaw/infer/model/bcs.tflite
```

(An **emulator build** still works via the HAL stubs — see `app/velapaw/README.md`.)

## ESP-NN note (reproducibility)

The ~1.3 s figure needs the **ESP-NN** SIMD kernels, which modify a **public** repo (`apps/mlearning/tflite-micro`). Per contest rules that change ships as a **fork/PR to `dev-ai-contest-2026`**, not vendored here — out of the box this repo runs the reference kernels (~6.75 s). Recipe + wrappers in `docs/esp-nn/`. See also `docs/ENGINEERING.md`.

Good news — you're clear to upload. Here's the full check against every constraint:

## Format / count / size ✅
- **13 STL files** (7 in `order1_mechanism`, 6 in `order2_structure`) — under the 20-file limit even if you upload both orders together.
- All **`.stl`** — the recommended format ✅
- Largest is `board_cradle_stand` at **1.0 MB** — nowhere near the 100 MB cap.

## Wall thickness — the "壁厚 > 1.2mm / 薄处 ≥ 0.8mm" rule
I audited the thickness parameters in the SCAD. **Every part clears it.** Thinnest feature in each:

| Part | Thinnest wall | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `board_cradle_stand` | lip face **1.6 mm**; pocket wall ~1.8 mm nominal (**1.3 mm** worst-case at FDM ±0.5) | ✅ tightest, still > 1.2 |
| `housing` | 3.0 mm | ✅ |
| `rotor` | vanes 3.0 mm | ✅ |
| `hopper` | cone ~2.1 mm | ✅ |
| `chute` | 2.0 mm floor + 2.0 mm rails | ✅ |
| `cam_pod` | front plate 2.0 mm, walls 2.5 mm, ears 3.0 mm | ✅ |
| `cam_mast` | pad 6 mm, legs 10×12 mm | ✅ |
| `plate_stepper` / `plate_idle` / `base_*` / `pedestal` / `support` | ≥ 3 mm | ✅ |

The single value worth knowing about is the **`board_cradle_stand` pocket wall** — nominally 1.8 mm but ~**1.3 mm worst-case** after FDM tolerance. That's above the 1.2 mm minimum (and well above the 0.8 mm thin-spot floor), and the design already deliberately grew it to stay in the safe band. It's the one part to glance at if the service flags anything.

## One honest caveat
These figures are the **design's nominal wall parameters**, not a mesh-level scan of the exported STLs. A CAD model can still produce a sub-1.2 mm *sliver* where two surfaces meet at a shallow angle — e.g. the rim of the lens-barrel hole on `cam_pod`, the FFC-slot lip, or a chamfer tip. Those services (this looks like JLC/等) **run their own thin-wall analysis on upload and highlight problem zones in red** — that auto-check is the authoritative one. If it flags a spot, tell me which part and I'll thicken it in the SCAD and re-export.

**Bottom line:** upload all 13 STLs (or the two orders separately if you want them billed apart) — they meet the format, count, size, and wall-thickness requirements. Want me to run an actual mesh wall-thickness scan locally before you commit, if you have a slicer/analysis tool I can call?

Short answer: **no — upload the STLs directly, not as a zip.**

Re-reading the service's own wording:

> 全彩打印可上传压缩文件 rar/zip

That zip/rar path is specifically for **全彩打印 (full-color printing)**. For standard single-material structural parts like yours (PLA/PETG/nylon), the normal flow is to **drag the individual `.stl` files in** — and they explicitly *recommend* STL. Zipping a normal order can either get rejected or misrouted into the color-print pipeline, and it also **hides each part from the per-file thin-wall analyzer** (the auto-check we just talked about runs per STL, not inside an archive).

So:
- You have **13 files ≤ 20** → just select/drag all 13 at once. No zip needed.
- Keep the **two orders separate** if you want them quoted/billed apart: upload the 7 `order1_mechanism` STLs as one order, the 6 `order2_structure` STLs as another. Otherwise all 13 in one upload is fine.

**Only** zip them if you're deliberately ordering **full-color** prints — and if that's the case, tell me and I'll package the exact STL set into a `.zip` for you.

163	  **wide-angle MAX OV5640 envelope** (14 mm square PCB, 15 mm barrel aperture)
164	  because the exact module was not calipered; a smaller real part just sits
165	  looser and is taken up by a bead of silicone from the open back. Nothing rigid
166	  touches the barrel — it may be an auto-focus VCM element that jams if pressed.
167	  The lens tip stands proud of the front plate, so even a 120° cone never
168	  vignettes. Two Ø3.4 ears bolt it to the yoke pad.
169	* **`cam_mast`** — a two-leg **yoke** (78 × 23 × 123 mm, ~36 cm³) that bolts to
170	  `base_front` with **2× M3** and stands **centred, straddling the chute**: the
171	  feet are at X ±34 (the trough is only X ±23), so the legs rise vertically
172	  *outboard* of the chute, then knee inward above the rails and each arm lands on
173	  its own ear of a tilted pad. That pad, built in the pod's own frame, carries the
174	  pod's two ears **just in front of the drum**, and is cut with a central
175	  **window** so the pod's open back stays open — that is how the OV5640 seats
176	  (drop the PCB in, silicone bead from behind) and how the FFC tail routes up past
177	  the pad. It is a **separate bolt-on part**, so the pedestal reverted to its
178	  plain 46 cm³ form.
179	
180	The pod sits central (X = 0), so the aim is a **pure steep down-tilt**: the pod
181	swings 180° about Z and tilts 68.3° about X to lay its lens onto the pet-face
182	target. The key trick is occlusion — a level camera here would shoot into the
183	back of the owner-facing screen, but from this low eye (z ≈ −13) the steep ray
184	drops below the screen's z = −20 bottom edge before reaching it and lands on the
185	pet over the bowl. Validated in the assembly by CGAL: pod, yoke and the aim
186	sightline each clear the board, hopper, drum, bowl, chute and pedestal (empty
187	intersections), and `cam_mast` is one closed solid (`Simple: yes`, one volume).
188	
189	**Caution — orientation before power.** A reversed FFC is fatal on first power:
190	board pin N mates camera pin 25−N, which puts a 1.5 V rail onto the camera's
191	ground and 2.8 V onto data lines. Before powering, buzz chassis ground to the
192	coupler's far contacts and confirm ground lands on the low-numbered (pin-2) end;
193	flip the cable if it shows at the pin-23/24 end.
194	
195	**Caliper note.** If the real module is measured, tightening `POD_PCB` in the
196	`.scad` re-exports **both** `cam_pod` and `cam_mast` — the yoke pad's hole
197	spacing tracks the pod outline (`EAR_X = POD_OUT/2 + POD_EAR_L/2`). Re-run the
198	two exports and the numbers above will shift slightly.
199	
200	## Pre-upload verification (measured on THESE files, not on the source)
201	
202	Run `verify_stl.py` and `bedcontact.py` against **each order folder** to
203	reproduce. Both folders were re-verified after the split — the checks below are
204	the union of the two runs, and nothing changed in the move.
205	
206	**Watertight — all 13 pass all four conditions.** "Watertight" is four separate
207	things, and a mesh can pass the naive check and still be rejected. The order2
208	files touched by the front-camera pivot (`base_front` gained 2 yoke-foot holes,
209	`pedestal` reverted, `cam_pod` unchanged, `cam_mast` the drum-front yoke) were re-verified by
210	CGAL (`Simple: yes`, one closed volume each) and z=0 seating:
211	
212	| Condition | Result |
213	|---|---|
214	| every edge shared by exactly 2 triangles (no holes/open edges) | 0 open edges |
215	| consistent winding — each directed edge used once | 0 bad |
216	| signed volume > 0 (normals point **out**, not in) | all positive |
217	| exactly 1 connected component per file | all 1 |
218	| zero-area/degenerate triangles | 0 |
219	
220	**Orientation — all 13 sit on z = 0.000 on a real FACE**, not an edge or a
221	vertex. First-layer contact area, which is the check that actually matters:
222	
223	| Part | bed contact | height |
224	|---|---|---|
225	| base_front | 28738 mm² (100% of footprint) | 15 |
226	| base_back | 14835 mm² (98%) | 15 |
227	| plate_idle | 4028 mm² (78%) | 11 |
228	| plate_stepper | 3904 mm² (75%) | 4 |
229	| support | 4652 mm² (31%) | 16 |
230	| rotor | 549 mm² (19%) | 38 |
231	| cam_pod | 208 mm² (front plate, 54%) | 8 |
232	| cam_mast | 240 mm² (2 feet, 100%) | 123 |
233	| housing | 629 mm² (15%) | 39.2 |
234	| hopper | 886 mm² (10%) | 80.7 |
235	| chute | 430 mm² (9%) | 92.5 |
236	| pedestal | 709 mm² | 102 |
237	| board_cradle_stand | 388 mm² (5%) | 81.0 |
238	
239	The **pedestal is back to 102 mm tall** — the camera gantry is gone, so the post
240	reverts to its plain form and lands on the same 709 mm² of foot pads at z=0.
241	`cam_mast` is a 123 mm two-leg yoke that stands on its two 10 × 12 feet (both flat
242	on z=0); on FDM the inward-leaning struts and the tilted pad at the top want
243	support, on MJF it is a non-issue.
244	
245	The low-ratio parts are tall and open by design; every one still lands on a flat
246	face. **On MJF none of this is binding** — it is a powder bed, JLC nest the parts
247	themselves, and there is no bed adhesion to lose. The poses are submitted correct
248	anyway because they make JLC's preview legible and they are what proves the set
249	could be made on a filament machine if it ever has to be.
250	
251	## Material volume — read this before ordering
252	
253	**632 cm³ total, ~0.63 kg of PA12** (includes support ×2). MJF is quoted mostly
254	by volume, so this is the number that sets the price. (Was 651 with the pedestal
255	gantry; the front-camera pivot dropped the gantry −55.5 cm³ off the pedestal and
256	added the `cam_mast` yoke +35.9 cm³, a net −20.)
257	
258	Nearly half of it is still the base plate:
259	
260	| | cm³ | share |
261	|---|---|---|
262	| base_front | 178.8 | 28% |
263	| base_back | 94.1 | 15% |
264	| **base plate subtotal** | **272.9** | **43%** |
265	| everything else (11 parts, 12 pieces) | 359.1 | 57% |
266	
267	By order: `order1_mechanism` 229 cm³ (36%), `order2_structure` 403 cm³ (64%).
268	The structure order is the bulkier one, and it carries the camera as well:
269	base plate 273, pedestal 46, board cradle 45, pod 2, yoke 36.
270	
271	**Per-order cost, using the recommended MJF/FDM split** (estimates in ¥; JLC
272	rates and region shift these, so treat as order-of-magnitude, and the 5-min
273	voucher check at the cart is what confirms them):
274	
275	| Order | Material | Volume | Est. before voucher | After −¥50 |
276	|---|---|---|---|---|
277	| `order1_mechanism` | **MJF PA12** | 229 cm³ | ~¥170–230 | ~¥120–180 |
278	| `order2_structure` | **FDM PLA/PETG** | 403 cm³ | ~¥90–120 | ~¥40–70 |
279	| **both** | | 632 cm³ | | **≈ ¥160–250** |
280	
281	For comparison: **all-FDM** ≈ ¥60–110 (weak fits on the mechanism), **all-MJF**
282	≈ ¥300–500 (overkill on the base plate). The split lands between the two and
283	puts the money where the tolerance actually matters. Watch the **second shipping
284	fee** — splitting adds one, and it comes off the ¥50 the second voucher gains.
285	
286	That base plate is a 5 mm solid floor over 164 × 176 and 164 × 92 mm.
287	
288	**DECIDED (2026-07-25): the base plate is being printed.** Substituting a cut
289	sheet of MDF or acrylic was considered and rejected, so the full base plate
290	stands (273 cm³ of the 632) and the two-order split holds as described above. Do
291	not re-open this at the cart.
292	
293	If volume ever does have to come out of it, the thing to know is that the floor
294	thickness is **not** a free parameter: the M3 × 12 countersunk tower screws are
295	dimensioned around exactly 5 mm (csk sinks 1.4, screw protrudes 7 into a 9 mm
296	flange). Thinning the floor means re-solving the screw stack. Pocketing or
297	ribbing the floor *between* the tower feet and the bowl ring is the change that
298	saves volume without touching the fastener scheme.
299	
300	## Sanity checks to run in JLC's uploader
301	
302	1. **Scale.** `velapaw_base_front_x1` must read ~**164 × 176 × 15 mm**. STL
303	   carries no units; if the viewer shows inches or centimetres the whole order
304	   is wrong by a constant factor and every part will be useless.
305	2. **Watertight / manifold.** All thirteen pass locally — CGAL reports
306	   `Simple: yes`, one closed volume, zero bad edges. If JLC's checker disagrees,
307	   suspect the upload, not the geometry.
308	3. **No trapped powder.** No part has an internal void, so there is nothing for
309	   un-sintered powder to be sealed inside. The deepest blind holes are the four
310	   ⌀1.7 × 12 pilots down the cradle posts, which are vestigial on the -C board
311	   (see `BM_SCREW_D` in the .scad) — they may be ignored or filled.
312	
313	## Fasteners — buy separately, NOT printed
314	
315	| Item | Qty | Where |
316	|---|---|---|
317	| M3 × 12 countersunk | 12 | towers → base plate (2 per foot, 6 feet) |
318	| M3 × 22 socket cap | 2 | base_front → base_back splice |
319	| M3 (plates → housing) | 8 | end plates onto the drum |
320	| M4 | 2 | 28BYJ-48 stepper flange |
321	| M3 × 8 self-tapping | 2 | camera pod → yoke pad (through Ø3.4 ears into Ø2.6 pilots) |
322	| M3 × 12 | 2 | camera yoke feet → base_front (Ø3.4 clearance, nut under the plate) |
323	
324	## After delivery
325	
326	The 28BYJ-48 D-shaft socket in the rotor is the one fit deliberately held
327	tighter than the MJF clearance rule, because it is the only joint transmitting
328	torque and slop there means mis-dosing. At the tight end of the tolerance it
329	will need a 5 mm drill run through by hand and a light file on the two flats.
330	Budget 30 seconds for it; it is intentional, not a defect.

I read your `ORDER.md` (the authoritative source) and cross-checked it against the screenshot. Mostly good, but there's **one thing you must fix before checkout.**

## 🔴 Must fix: `support` quantity = 2
Order 1 is **7 files but 8 pieces** — `velapaw_support` needs **quantity 2**, everything else is ×1. The screenshot shows the visible rows (chute/hopper/housing) all at 数量 **1**, which is correct for them, but scroll down to **`velapaw_support_x2.stl`** and set its 数量 to **2**.

This is the one part your own order notes flag in bold:
> `support` is the only part with quantity 2 — the drum sits in an A-frame at each end… a missing A-frame means the machine **cannot be assembled at all.**

The `_x2` in the filename is exactly the reminder for this. Currently it looks like it'll default to 1.

## ✅ What checks out
- **7 parts selected** = the correct Order 1 set (已选中 7 款零件).
- **Scale is correct** (the #1 thing that ruins an STL order). Your files read in the right magnitude — I verified two exactly against the model: hopper `8.07×9.6×9.6 cm` = 80.7×96×96 mm ✓, housing `3.92×6.4×6.4 cm` = 39.2×64×64 mm ✓. Reading as **cm, not inches** — good.
- The **openvela voucher** is applied (优惠券 openvela…打样券) — that's one of the two ¥50 coupons; save the other for Order 2.

## ⚠️ Worth a second thought: material = 9600 (resin)
You've picked **9600 / 哑光白** — that's an **SLA resin**. Two implications for *this* order specifically (the mechanism):
- **Fits:** fine — resin is *more* accurate than FDM, so the rotor/housing/A-frame clearances (sized for ±0.5 FDM) will be comfortable, not tight. ✅
- **Strength:** standard resin is **brittle**. This order carries the load-bearing parts — the rotor's D-shaft **torque socket**, the running fit in the housing, and the **A-frame supports** holding the drum. Your `ORDER.md` recommends **MJF PA12 nylon** for exactly this mechanism order for that reason.

For a **样品 / demo** (which is what this quote is) resin is acceptable and looks clean. But if this is meant to be the **functional feeder** that actually turns kibble, nylon (MJF) or PLA/PETG would survive the torque and repeated use far better. Your call — just flagging it while you're still at the cart.

**Bottom line:** set `support` to **qty 2**, decide resin-vs-nylon, then this order is good to place. Want me to double-check Order 2's quantities and material recommendation the same way when you get to it?
so what should it be changed to on the material

For **Order 1 (the mechanism)**, change it from **9600 (resin)** to:

## → 尼龙 PA12 (Nylon PA12 / MJF)

That's the material your `ORDER.md` specifies for this order, and it's the right call because Order 1 holds the **load-bearing, torque-transmitting parts** — the rotor's D-shaft socket, the running fit in the housing, and the A-frame supports. Nylon PA12:
- **Doesn't snap** under torque/repeated use (resin does — that's the whole concern)
- Is **dimensionally accurate** (your fits were sized for it)
- Is slightly flexible, washable, and inert — good for a kibble mechanism

On JLC's dropdown look for **"尼龙 PA12"** / **"MJF 尼龙"** / **"选择性激光烧结 (SLS)"** — same part family, that's the one to pick.

### If PA12 is too pricey or you want to stay in the resin flow
Second-best, in order:
1. **韧性树脂 / 类尼龙树脂** (tough / nylon-like resin, e.g. JLC's 8228-type) — far less brittle than 9600, decent for a functional demo.
2. **FDM PETG or PLA** — cheapest, tough enough for a working demo; PETG if you want it a bit more durable.

**Avoid** standard brittle resins (9600, 8000/8001 general-purpose) for anything in Order 1.

### Important: this only applies to Order 1
For **Order 2 (structure)** — base plate, pedestal, cradle, cam mount — there are **no printed-to-printed fits** and nothing takes torque; they just bolt together with M3s. So for Order 2, **cheap FDM PLA/PETG is fine**, and even 9600 resin would be acceptable there. That's exactly why `ORDER.md` recommends the split: **PA12 nylon for Order 1, cheap FDM for Order 2** — money spent only where strength and tolerance actually matter.

So: **Order 1 → Nylon PA12.** Want me to note the recommended material on each part when you set up Order 2?

text:
Read the cradle's numbers, and here's the honest picture — the cradle's problem is **not** thinness:

## The cradle passed the thin-wall check — its flag was 易变形 (warp risk)
Its locating walls are already deliberately sized: `BM_WALL = 2.8` nominal, which prints to **1.8 mm** (1.3 mm at the worst corner). The SCAD comments show this was tuned *on purpose* to clear "**JLCPCB's 1.2 mm FDM minimum**" with margin ([velapaw_feeder.scad:516-524](D:\openVela\contest2026_043_CircuitForge\hardware\velapaw_feeder.scad#L516-L524)). So the walls aren't too thin — that's why JLC gave it a green ✅ on 薄壁结构.

What it *did* flag is **易变形结构 (deformation-prone)**, and that's a different problem. It comes from the **shape**: a tall, thin pocket wall (`BM_WALL_H = 14` mm high × 1.8 mm thin) running all the way around a big 95×64 tray, sitting on an open-leg tilted stand. In **SLA resin (9600)** a shape like that genuinely warps as it cures and in transit — exactly what the red banner on the material screen warned about. Thickening one rib won't change the fundamental warp tendency.

## The real fix for the cradle: print it in nylon, not resin
This is the one Order-2 part where I'd **not** use cheap resin:

1. **Best — move just the cradle to 尼龙 PA12 (MJF).** Nylon is dimensionally stable and doesn't warp on flat/tall spans the way resin does — it kills the 易变形 risk directly. And this is the part that **locates your ESP32 screen**, so stability matters more here than on any other bracket. MJF's min wall is ~1.0 mm, so the existing 1.3 mm corner is fine as-is. Put the cradle in the Order-1 nylon batch, or just select nylon for it.

2. **If you want to keep it cheap** — two sub-options:
   - **接受风险 (accept risk)** on resin: for a static demo it'll probably hold the board even with slight warp.
   - **Or I stiffen it in CAD:** bump `BM_WALL` 2.8 → ~4.0 (printed wall 1.8 → ~3.0 mm) so those tall pocket walls resist warping, then re-export. That's a real anti-warp change I can make — but it's still second-best to just using nylon.

**One bonus:** the cradle's fits (`BM_FIT = 2.0`, the wall sizing) were tuned for FDM's loose ±0.5 mm. Switch it to nylon (±0.3) or resin (±0.2) and the board fits *more* easily, not less — so changing material here has no downside on the board seating.

### My call
Print the **cradle in PA12 nylon** — cleanest fix, no CAD change needed, and it's the part where accuracy earns its keep. Everything else in Order 2 (base, pedestal, cam mount) can stay cheap resin/FDM.

Want me to (a) just move the cradle to nylon and leave the geometry alone, or (b) *also* thicken `BM_WALL` to 4.0 as belt-and-suspenders before you re-export?

import sys, trimesh, numpy as np

def report(tag, m):
    print(f"  [{tag}] faces={len(m.faces)} verts={len(m.vertices)} "
          f"watertight={m.is_watertight} winding_consistent={m.is_winding_consistent} "
          f"vol={m.volume:.2f}mm^3")

for path in sys.argv[1:]:
    print(f"\n=== {path} ===")
    m = trimesh.load(path, process=True)
    if isinstance(m, trimesh.Scene):
        m = trimesh.util.concatenate(tuple(m.geometry.values()))
    report("before", m)
    before_ok = m.is_winding_consistent
    # merge coincident verts, drop degenerate/duplicate faces, then re-orient
    m.merge_vertices()
    m.update_faces(m.nondegenerate_faces())
    m.update_faces(m.unique_faces())
    m.remove_infinite_values()
    m.fix_normals()          # make winding consistent + normals outward
    report("after ", m)
    out = path.replace(".stl", "_fixed.stl")
    m.export(out)
    print(f"  fixed winding: {before_ok} -> {m.is_winding_consistent}   wrote {out}")

That "defect" verdict was my bad logic — `verts=1476 = 492×3` and `watertight=False` is just how **every** binary STL looks unwelded; STL has no shared vertices by format. The *welded* topology (what any slicer reconstructs) is the perfect one: **euler=2, watertight, single body, consistent outward winding.** That mesh has no reversed faces — it's mathematically impossible for it to.

Here's the key evidence chain:

- The pedestal is a **provably correct, printable mesh** by every rigorous test.
- **JLC's own auto-repair fails** ("修复模型失败") — because there's nothing to repair.
- It re-flags even my freshly re-welded binary export with identical geometry.

**This is a false positive in JLC's auto-checker.** Its heuristic is misreading the pedestal/chute's open, concave geometry (legs, archway, mounting cutouts) as "reversed faces." No amount of mesh surgery fixes a checker that's wrong about a correct mesh — and you can see that in the fact that JLC's *own* repair gives up on it.

## What to actually do: stop using the repair tool — place the order with manual review

The repair page (`modelRepair`) is a dead end here. Go back to the **order/checkout** and use **人工审核下单 ("place order with manual review")**. The orange banner on the anomaly dialog literally says:
> 最终以人工审核信息为准 — *the final determination is made by human review.*

That's the designed escape hatch for exactly this: a part the robot flags but a human can see prints fine. JLC's engineers will look at the pedestal, confirm it's a clean solid, and print it. This applies to **both the chute and the pedestal** (both are the open/concave "tower" parts the checker trips on).

### So, concretely:

Done — the stand is now at **maximum reasonable stiffness**. Here's the complete answer to "is there nothing we can do":

## Everything that's now IN the stand (v3)

| Measure | v1 (flagged) | v3 (now) |
|---|---|---|
| Pocket/leg walls | 1.8 mm printed | **3.0 mm** |
| Tray floor | 3 mm | **4 mm** |
| Rear stretcher | none (open legs) | **35 mm shear web** — closed portal frame |
| Volume / stiffness mass | 45.5 cm³ | **81.0 cm³** (+78 %) |

One catch my check caught before it bit you: thickening the floor lengthens the camera-window bore, and by the design's own formula the 72° FOV cone then needs 23.2 mm — the old 22 mm window would have **vignetted the corners of every frame** (silently degrading the pet detector). Window widened to 24 mm in step. That's exactly the kind of coupling that makes "just thicken it" dangerous — it's handled.

**Upload:** `fixed_reupload/velapaw_board_cradle_stand_v3_x1.stl` (new filename → fresh robot check, no cache).

## Straight answer on expectations
That's the end of what geometry can do. If v3 *still* shows 易变形, it's the checker classifying "tilted tray on legs in resin" as a category, not measuring your part — at that point the flag doesn't go away by design, only by one of:

1. **接受风险** — now genuinely safe: this is a closed-frame part with 3–4 mm sections, and JLC themselves say minor resin warp corrects with warm water.
2. **Print this one part in 尼龙 PA12** — nylon doesn't warp, and the flag logic is aimed at resin. At 81 cm³ nylon will cost noticeably more, but it's the part that holds your screen.

My call: upload v3, and if the flag persists, accept risk — the engineering is real now, the flag would just be the category label. Fit-wise nothing changed for mating parts: same footprint on the pedestal rails, same board pocket, stretcher inside the outline.

Confirmed in firmware (`rotor_index_one` swept 60° and back). A stepper rotates CONTINUOUSLY one direction → pockets ratchet inlet→outlet → true per-pocket dosing, and "grams = pockets × GRAMS_PER_POCKET" becomes literally true. Geared 28BYJ-48 also has strong low-speed torque (resists kibble jams).

42	- Board: ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5-C (camera+case included).
43	- **Servo (dispenser):** continuous-rotation micro servo **FS90R** (gentle, ~5V) driving a 3D-printed auger; or MG996R (more torque, needs its own supply). Single servo = single PWM pin.
44	- **Separate 5 V ≥2 A supply** for the servo + **~1000 µF cap** across it; common ground with the board. Do NOT power the servo from the board's 3.3V/LCD rail.
45	- **microSD card** (for persistent feed history).
46	- Jumper wires, M3 screws / heat-set inserts.
47	- **3D-printed (user has a print coupon):** hopper + lid, auger + tube, chute, bowl (or bowl mount), camera/board mount aiming the camera at the bowl, main enclosure.
48	
49	## Pinout (from the official ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-3.5 schematic)
50	Board is nearly fully pinned. Native GPIO map:
51	- LCD (ST7796 SPI): IO1 MOSI, IO2 MISO, IO3 DC, IO4 (QSPI IO3), IO5 SCLK, IO6 BL
52	- I2C bus (touch/RTC/IMU/audio/AXP shared): **IO7 SCL, IO8 SDA**
53	- SD card (SPI): IO9 MISO, IO10 MOSI, IO11 SCLK  (SD_CS on expander EXIO3)
54	- I2S audio (ES8311): IO12 MCLK, IO13 SCLK, IO14 ASDOUT, IO15 LRCK, IO16 DSDIN
55	- Camera (OV5640 DVP): IO17 VSYNC, IO18 HREF, IO21 D7, IO38 XCLK, IO39 D6, IO40 D5, IO41 PCLK, IO42 D4, IO45 D0, IO46 D3, IO47 D1, IO48 D2
56	- USB-C: IO19 (D-), IO20 (D+)
57	- UART0 console: IO43 TXD, IO44 RXD
58	- Flash + octal PSRAM: IO26–37 region (reserved)
59	- IO0: IMU INT + strapping (avoid)
60	- TCA9554 expander EXIO0–7 (all used): CAM_PWDN, LCD_RST, TP_INT, SD_CS, RTC_INT, AXP_IRQ, SYS_OUT, PA_CTRL. Expander is I2C → cannot do servo PWM.
61	
62	## SERVO WIRING DECISION
63	There is **no idle native GPIO** except the UART pins. Plan:
64	- **Servo signal → GPIO43** (LEDC hardware PWM). (GPIO44 available as a 2nd actuator if ever needed.)
65	- **Free IO43/44 by moving the debug console to USB** — use the ESP32-S3 built-in **USB-Serial/JTAG over the USB-C** (IO19/20) instead of UART0. Keeps full logging.
66	- **Servo power: separate 5 V + common ground** (see BOM). Flash/logs over USB-C.
67	- Do NOT use the TCA9554 expander for the servo (I2C too slow for 50 Hz PWM).
68	
69	## Features this board unlocks (deferred in emulator)
70	- **RTC (PCF85063)** → real **meal-timing** (was skipped for lack of a wall clock).
71	- **microSD** → **persistent feed history / analytics** across reboots (was in-memory only).
72	
73	## Feeder dispensing — grams -> motion (calibration)
74	The app speaks **grams** (portions ~5-50g, daily limits 20-300g; NOT kg). The dispenser does not measure grams; it is CALIBRATED once:
75	- Measure kibble released per unit of motion: run the auger 1 rotation (or motor 1 s), weigh the output on a kitchen scale -> e.g. `grams_per_rotation` ~= 5g (or `grams_per_second` ~= 8g). Store the constant (NVS/SD so it survives reboot).
76	- **Dispense N grams = run actuator for N / grams_per_unit** (e.g. 20g @ 5g/rot = 4 rotations, or 2.5s @ 8g/s).
77	- This is OPEN-LOOP feeding (no sensor): ~±10-20% accurate, standard for consumer feeders. Fine for v1.
78	
79	**Firmware hook:** `velapaw_feeder_dispense(grams)` (currently mock print) becomes on hardware: `runtime = grams / grams_per_second; drive_servo(GPIO43 LEDC PWM, runtime);`. Nothing above it changes (app stays in grams). Planned backend: hal/feeder_servo.c.
80	
81	**Accuracy upgrade (deferred):** add a **load cell + HX711** under the bowl -> CLOSED-LOOP: dispense until measured weight == target (~1g accurate). Same hardware also gives real EATEN-grams / eating-speed (the analytics we deferred). Needs the load cell (not on the board).
82	
83	**Suggested (not yet built):** a UI "Calibrate" mode = dispense a test amount -> user weighs it -> enter value -> stores grams_per_unit.

text:
Short answer: **that exact sentence, no** — but voice-scheduling, yes, and you're closer than you'd think. I dug through the tree to check rather than guess. Two hard blockers, one of which is a genuine surprise.

## What's already in your favor (verified)

| Piece | Status |
|---|---|
| `nuttx/drivers/audio/es8311.c` | Supports `AUDIO_TYPE_INPUT` — mic capture, not just playback |
| `nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/esp32s3_i2s.c` | `i2s_receive()` + `CONFIG_ESP32S3_I2S0_RX` present |
| `apps/audioutils/speexdsp` | VAD, noise suppression, AGC — the frontend you'd otherwise write |
| TFLM + ESP-NN on your board | **This is your ASR engine.** Already debugged. |
| `external/bailian_sdk/libs/libc_mmi_cmd_voice_translate.a` | Alibaba Qwen/Bailian voice SDK, already vendored |

## Blocker 1: your stepper is sitting on the microphone bus

This is the real problem. `board/esp32s3_st7789.c:385-388`:

```c
#define STEP_IN1  12   /* ES8311 MCLK  (unused audio) */
#define STEP_IN2  13   /* ES8311 SCLK  (unused audio) */
#define STEP_IN3  15   /* ES8311 LRCK  (unused audio) */
#define STEP_IN4  16   /* ES8311 DSDIN (unused audio) */
```

Mic capture needs **12 (MCLK), 13 (BCLK), 15 (LRCK), 14 (ASDOUT)**. Three of the four are held by the motor. And you can't time-share them — while I²S clocks the lines at MHz, your ULN2003 sees that as coil drive and the motor buzzes and heats.

**Fix: move the stepper to an I²C GPIO expander** (PCF8574, ~¥3, on the existing IO7/IO8 bus).

Your hardware notes say *"Do NOT use the TCA9554 expander for the servo (I²C too slow for 50 Hz PWM)."* **That reasoning doesn't carry to the stepper.** A servo needs µs-accurate pulse widths 50×/sec — I²C jitter destroys it. A stepper just needs a coil pattern updated at `STEP_DELAY_US=1500` ≈ 667 writes/sec, one byte each, ~60 µs at 400 kHz. About 4% bus load, and timing jitter costs you nothing but a hair of smoothness. The old objection was correct for the part you no longer use.

Related: that file still says `STEP_IN4 16` while your verified wiring is GPIO43 — still unreconciled. If the stepper moves to an expander, all four defines change anyway, so this decision supersedes that nit.

## Blocker 2: does the board actually have a mic?

**Unverified.** There is no microphone reference anywhere in your repo, and your pinout notes list ES8311 but never a mic. ES8311 is a *codec* — it needs an analog mic on its MIC input. Check the schematic PDF you already used for the camera connector work: look for a MEMS part near ES8311, or a `MIC1P`/`MIC1N` net. If it's absent, an electret capsule is a ~¥2 add. **Verify this before anything else** — it's the one item that can kill the whole idea.

## What voice can realistically do

**Not on-device:** free-form "velapaw schedule the first feeding time for pet king at 8" as one utterance. That's large-vocabulary continuous ASR plus NLU. The S3 can't, and there's no ASR engine anywhere in openVela — you'd be building from zero.

**Tier 1 — TFLM keyword spotting (my recommendation).** Google's micro_speech architecture: 40-bin MFCC over a 1 s window → small CNN, 20–40 KB. On your ESP-NN build, tens of milliseconds — noise next to your 1310 ms pet inference. Budget 10–20 words. You don't say the sentence, you walk a tree:

> "Hi VelaPaw" → *beep* → "schedule" → *screen lists pets* → "King" → "breakfast" → "eight" ✓

Each turn is a 3–8 word decision — exactly what small KWS is good at — and the LCD shows what's sayable, so the user is never guessing. That's a real product interaction, not a downgrade.

**Tier 2 — cloud, for your literal sentence.** Wake word on-device, then stream ~3 s of PCM to Qwen via `external/bailian_sdk`, get back `{action, pet, meal, hour}`. Gets you the exact phrasing. Costs WiFi + an API key + latency. For a contest judged on *on-device* AI, build Tier 1 first and offer this as an optional online mode.

**Tier 3 — ESP-SR (WakeNet/MultiNet).** Don't. Closed binary libs built against ESP-IDF's FreeRTOS/heap APIs; you're on NuttX with no IDF shim in the tree. Open-ended porting risk.

## Sequencing, and the honest schedule warning

This is a big addition — expander rework, rewiring, audio bring-up, model training, a dialog state machine, UI. Your parts aren't printed yet and the stepper isn't confirmed on final wiring. I'd gate it hard:

1. **Confirm the mic exists** on the schematic (30 min, decides everything)
2. **Move the stepper to the PCF8574**, prove it still turns
3. **Record a WAV to SD and play it back on your PC** — until raw capture is clean, a model is premature
4. *Only then* train keywords

If step 1 or 3 stalls, you've lost a day, not the project. Want me to start with the schematic check, or scope out the pin migration properly?

text:
Good — then the ES8311 route is off the table, and that turns out to be *better*. I went looking for what the firmware actually claims, and both blockers I raised dissolve.

## The finding

From `board/configs/waveshare_lcd/defconfig`:

```
CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_CLKPIN=5
CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_CSPIN=4
CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MISOPIN=-1     ← MISO disabled: GPIO2 is free
CONFIG_ESP32S3_SPI2_MOSIPIN=1
```

And there is **no `MMCSD`, no `SDMMC`, no `I2S`, no `AUDIO`, no `ES8311` anywhere in that defconfig.** The microSD slot is populated in hardware but your firmware never touches it — GPIO 9/10/11 are unclaimed.

| Pin | Nominal use | Actually used by firmware? |
|---|---|---|
| **GPIO2** | LCD MISO | **No** — explicitly `-1` |
| **GPIO9/10/11** | microSD SPI | **No** — no SD config exists |
| GPIO4 | (notes said "QSPI IO3") | **Yes** — it's the LCD chip-select |

Four free native pins, none of them anywhere near the motor.

## So: bring your own microphone

Skip the ES8311 entirely. An **external I²S MEMS mic** — INMP441 or SPH0645, ~¥6, 3 signal wires — talks straight to the S3's **I2S0**, which is a separate peripheral from the pins your stepper occupies.

`nuttx/arch/xtensa/src/esp32s3/Kconfig` confirms the pins are yours to pick:

```
ESP32S3_I2S0_BCLKPIN / _WSPIN / _DINPIN   (free ints, GPIO-matrix routed)
ESP32S3_I2S0_MCLK                          (bool — optional; INMP441 doesn't need it)
```

Three pins, and you have four. What this buys you:

- **Motor untouched** — GPIO 12/13/15/16 stay exactly as wired and coded
- **Blocker 2 is gone** — no longer matters whether the board has an onboard mic; you're supplying one
- **Better audio anyway** — a digital MEMS mic beats an electret through a codec, and I²S RX is a far shorter path than codec bring-up

⚠️ One rule to add to your list, alongside the CONFIG_RTC one: **never enable `CONFIG_AUDIO_ES8311` or the board's `esp32s3_es8311.c` glue.** That code would bring up the codec on I²S pins 12/13/15/16 and start clocking your stepper coils. Raw I2S0 + digital mic only.

## The one thing left to verify

Are GPIO 2 / 9 / 10 / 11 **broken out on the 2×16 header?** GPIO2 runs to the LCD FPC; 9/10/11 run to the microSD slot. Free in software ≠ reachable with a jumper. Check the same schematic you used for the camera connector — that's a 20-minute answer.

If they're *not* on the header, there's a solder-free escape: a **microSD extender/sniffer board** (~¥8) plugs into the slot and breaks CLK/CMD/DAT0 out to a header. Three pins, no iron, motor still untouched.

The software plan from before is unchanged — TFLM keyword spotting on your existing ESP-NN stack, walked as a short dialog tree rather than one long sentence. Want me to check the schematic for those four pins?

Confirmed — the page settles it. From "What's On Board":

- **16. Microphone** ✅ (analog, into the ES8311)
- **14. ES8311** low-power audio codec
- **7. MX1.25 speaker header**, and the box ships a **6Ω 1W speaker**
- Banner: *"Integrated audio input and output, enabling AI interaction and offline voice control"*

So the hardware you need is already sitting on the board, free, no soldering. That kills the "is there a mic" question dead.

## But it changes nothing about the pin problem

The onboard mic is wired to the **ES8311**, and the ES8311 lives on I²S at GPIO 12/13/14/15/16. Capture needs **MCLK(12), BCLK(13), LRCK(15), ASDOUT(14)** — and your stepper is sitting on 12, 13, and 15.

There's no clever way around it. The GPIO matrix can route I²S to those pins from either peripheral, but the ULN2003 is still physically attached to them. Using the onboard mic means the stepper moves. Full stop.

So your "don't touch the motor" constraint now has a real, quantifiable price:

| | Onboard mic (ES8311) | External MEMS mic |
|---|---|---|
| Motor | **Must move** (→ PCF8574) | Untouched |
| Cost | ¥0 | ~¥6 + wiring |
| Mic | Already there | You add it |
| **Speaker** | **Works** — free, in the box | **Not available** |
| Audio feedback | Beeps, spoken confirmations | Screen only |

The speaker is the part worth pausing on. Voice UIs lean hard on audio confirmation — a chirp when the wake word lands, a tone when a command is accepted. Without it you're mute.

**That said, I don't think it's fatal for you.** You have a 3.5" touch LCD pointed right at the user. A big "🎤 Listening…" panel, the recognized word echoed back in large type, a green flash on accept — that's arguably *better* feedback than a beep, and it fits the guided dialog tree from before, where the screen already has to show what's sayable. The external-mic path is a real product, not a crippled one.

## One warning about the marketing

The page advertises *"offline voice control"* and *"AI Speech Interaction — DeepSeek, Doubao."* That's **ESP-IDF + ESP-SR**, Espressif's stack. You're on openVela/NuttX. None of that transfers — the ESP-SR libraries are closed binaries built against IDF's FreeRTOS and heap APIs. So "the board supports offline voice control" is true of the silicon, not of your firmware. Either path still means building keyword spotting yourself on the TFLM stack you already have running.

## My call

Given you don't want to touch the motor: **external I²S MEMS mic on GPIO 2/9/10/11, screen for feedback.** ~¥6, motor untouched, and the software plan is identical either way.

But it's worth knowing you're paying ¥6 and a free speaker to avoid rewiring four jumper wires — and that the expander move is genuinely low-risk (~4% I²C bus load, and the "too slow" objection in your notes was written about the servo, not the stepper). If you'd reconsider once the boards are assembled and you're already wiring, say so and I'll scope it properly.

Short answer: **not for the part that's actually blocking you.**

## What a breadboard can't fix

The open question is *"do GPIO 2 / 9 / 10 / 11 physically reach the 2×16 header?"* A breadboard sits downstream of that. If GPIO9/10/11 terminate at the microSD slot and GPIO2 at the LCD FPC and never reach a header pin, there is nothing on the board to plug a jumper into — a breadboard just gives you a nicer place to land wires that don't exist yet.

I checked for a local schematic; there isn't one in the repo (`docs/` has only reports). So that verification still needs the Waveshare PDF or a continuity meter on the actual header.

## Where a breadboard doesn't help either

For the mic itself you don't want one. An INMP441 breakout has six 0.1" pins (VDD, GND, SD, SCK, WS, L/R) and your board has a 0.1" header — **six female-to-female jumpers connect them directly.** A breadboard would insert two extra spring contacts per signal for zero benefit.

And you have specific history here. Your SPI-LCD partial-window bug ended up being *wire-level, needs a logic analyzer* — days lost to a physical-layer ghost. I²S BCLK at 16 kHz × 64 = ~1 MHz is well within what a breadboard can carry, so it's not a bandwidth problem, but every added contact is another candidate for that same class of intermittent fault. On a bring-up you're going to be debugging blind, fewer joints is strictly better.

## Where one genuinely earns its place

**Power and ground distribution.** You have a real star-ground problem brewing:

- separate 5 V ≥2 A supply → ULN2003 → 28BYJ-48
- 1000 µF bulk cap across that rail
- board 3.3 V → mic VDD
- **all grounds common**

That's four or five things that need to meet at one ground node, and twisting bare wires together is exactly how you get a motor-noise problem that looks like a firmware bug. A breadboard's power rails solve that cleanly — and the stepper's coil current is well under what breadboard rails handle.

So: **yes for the power/ground rails, no for the mic signals, and irrelevant to the header question.**

Want me to pull the Waveshare schematic and settle GPIO 2/9/10/11 pin-by-pin? That's the thing standing between you and ordering parts, and I've flagged it twice without going to get it.

That schematic reverses my recommendation. Reading the netlist directly:

## The 2×16 header (J8), fully decoded

| | | | |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** VBAT | **2** VBUS | **17** IO45 `CAM_D0` | **18** IO18 `CAM_HREF` |
| **3** GND | **4** GND | **19** IO46 `CAM_D3` | **20** IO0 `IMU_INT`/strap |
| **5** IO21 `CAM_D7` | **6** USB_N | **21** IO47 `CAM_D1` | **22** EN |
| **7** IO38 `CAM_XCLK` | **8** USB_P | **23** IO48 `CAM_D2` | **24** PWRON |
| **9** IO39 `CAM_D6` | **10** IO11 `SD_SCLK` | **25** IO44 `U0RXD` | **26** IO7 `SCL` |
| **11** IO40 `CAM_D5` | **12** IO10 `SD_MOSI` | **27** IO43 `U0TXD` | **28** IO8 `SDA` |
| **13** IO41 `CAM_PCLK` | **14** IO9 `SD_MISO` | **29** GND | **30** GND |
| **15** IO42 `CAM_D4` | **16** IO17 `CAM_VSYNC` | **31** 3V3 | **32** 3V3 |

## Three findings, in order of impact

**1. IO12/13/14/15/16 are not on the header at all.** Every one of those nets has exactly two nodes — the ESP32 and the ES8311:

```
PIU1017 PIU702   NLIO12 NLI2S0MCLK      ← U1.17 + U7.2, nothing else
PIU1018 PIU706   NLIO13 NLI2S0SCLK
PIU1019 PIU707   NLIO14 NLI2S0ASDOUT
PIU1021 PIU708   NLIO15 NLI2S0LRCK
PIU1022 PIU709   NLIO16 NLI2S0DSDIN
```

The codec bus is **private**. No wire can reach it — which means **no wire can conflict with it either.**

**2. GPIO2 is dead.** `NLIO2 / NLLCD0SPI0MISO` has a single node: U1 pin 7. It isn't on the header *and* it isn't on the LCD connector — the LCD's SDO (L1.22) is likewise dangling. Waveshare simply never routed the display read-back line. That's why `MISOPIN=-1`. It's an unbonded dead end; forget it.

**3. GPIO 9/10/11 *are* on the header — pins 14, 12, 10 — and your stepper already owns them.** Your bring-up note has it: `IN1=GPIO9, IN2=GPIO10, IN3=GPIO11, IN4=GPIO43`. All four are header pins (14, 12, 10, 27). That's the real wiring.

## So the conclusion flips — in your favor

I told you the onboard mic was unreachable because the stepper sat on the codec's I²S bus. **It doesn't.** The stepper is on 9/10/11/43; the codec bus is on 12–16 where no jumper can go.

| | Before this PDF | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| Onboard mic + speaker | "blocked by motor" | **Free. Zero motor changes.** |
| External MEMS mic | "the recommended path" | **Impossible — no free pins left** |

Free header GPIOs after the stepper: IO44 (clamped, useless as an output — you proved that), IO0 (strapping + IMU INT). That's it. There is nowhere to put an external mic. The path I recommended is gone, and the one I ruled out is the only one that works — and it's better: ¥0, no soldering, and you get the **speaker** too.

Everything else checks out on the audio side: the mic is analog differential into `MIC1P`/`MIC1N` through R41/R43; the speaker runs through an **NS4150B** amp whose enable is `PA_CTRL` on **EXIO7** of the TCA9554 you already drive; and codec control (`AU_SCL`/`AU_SDA`) is on the **same IO7/IO8 I²C bus** as your touch, RTC, and expander. Nothing new to wire.

## It also explains the buzz saga

With `STEP_IN1/2/3 = 12/13/15`, three of the four coils were driving pins that terminate at the codec and reach no header pin at all. Only IN4 was ever electrically connected. **That's why it vibrated instead of turning** — no coil sequence could have fixed it. GPIO44 was a second, real fault stacked on top.

## One thing to fix, and it's now load-bearing

[board/esp32s3_st7789.c:385-388](board/esp32s3_st7789.c#L385-L388) still says `12 / 13 / 15 / 16`. The repo copy never got the bring-up edit (the VM tree isn't on this machine, so the working version lives only there). That was a cosmetic nit yesterday. It isn't anymore: **the moment you enable the ES8311, `step_coils()` starts hammering MCLK, SCLK, LRCK and DSDIN on every dispense.** Feeding would corrupt audio and audio would corrupt feeding.

Correct it to `9 / 10 / 11 / 43`, plus the comment at line 889 and the stale note in [docs/SESSION_STATE.md:26](docs/SESSION_STATE.md#L26).

Want me to make that edit and update `velapaw-hardware.md`? Its pinout section is wrong in three places now — GPIO4 as "QSPI IO3", GPIO2 as LCD MISO, and "no idle native GPIO" — and the full J8 map plus "the codec bus is private" are worth keeping.

Depends which "it." Two very different confidence levels.

## First — retract something I told you

I said: *"never enable `CONFIG_AUDIO_ES8311` or the board's `esp32s3_es8311.c` glue — it would clock the stepper coils."* That was built on the wrong pin map. The stepper isn't on those pins. **Enabling that glue is now the recommended path**, not a forbidden one. Ignore the rule; I never wrote it to memory, so nothing downstream is contaminated.

## Getting audio running: high confidence

Better than I expected. `nuttx/boards/xtensa/esp32s3/common/src/esp32s3_es8311.c` already exists, upstream-maintained, gated on `CONFIG_ESP32S3_I2S && CONFIG_AUDIO_ES8311`. You aren't writing a codec driver — you're turning on config and calling `esp32s3_es8311_initialize()`. Combined with `es8311.c` supporting `AUDIO_TYPE_INPUT` and `i2s_receive()` being present, "capture PCM from the onboard mic" is a config-and-glue job.

Real risks, all ordinary:
- **Config landmines.** Your track record here is bad — `CONFIG_RTC` killed the USB console. Audio pulls in the scheduler/workqueue and a chunk of the audio subsystem. Turn it on alone first and confirm the console still comes up before doing anything else.
- **The board's I²S0 pins must be pinned to 12/13/14/15/16 in defconfig.** Defaults are 4/5, which collide with your LCD CS and SCLK. This is the one place where a wrong config *does* break the display.
- **MCLK.** ES8311 needs it; `ESP32S3_I2S0_MCLK` must be on, MCLKPIN=12.

I'd put getting a `.wav` recorded off the mic at **high probability, a session or two of work.**

## Voice recognition: that's the actual project

The pin problem was never the hard part — it was just the part blocking everything. Here's what's genuinely unsolved:

- **No ASR engine in the tree.** Nothing. You build keyword spotting on TFLM yourself.
- **No MFCC frontend.** The 40-bin filterbank that turns audio into model input doesn't exist in your tree either. That's real DSP code, and it runs on every frame, continuously.
- **No model, and no training data.** `micro_speech` is a reference for *yes/no/unknown*. A vocabulary of "VelaPaw / schedule / King / breakfast / eight" means collecting samples and training. This is the bulk of the work, and it's off-device work — days, not hours.
- **Continuous CPU cost.** KWS is cheap per inference but never stops. It shares a core with LVGL, the camera pipeline, and your 1310 ms recognition model. Feasible, but you'll be tuning contention.

And the original ask stands unchanged: **"velapaw schedule the first feeding time for pet king at 8" will not work as a spoken sentence on-device.** That's free-form ASR + NLU. On-device you get a guided dialog tree; the literal sentence needs cloud, via `external/bailian_sdk`.

## Straight answer

The hardware question is **settled yes** — mic, speaker, codec, no motor conflict, no new parts, no rewiring. That's a genuine unblock and it cost you nothing.

Whether *voice control* ships is a schedule question, not a feasibility one. It's a new subsystem — DSP frontend, a trained model, a dialog UI — bolted onto a project whose enclosure isn't assembled and whose JLC reorders are still open. **I'd treat it as a stretch feature, not a committed one.**

Cheapest way to find out: enable the codec, record and play back a `.wav`. That's a few hours, it de-risks every config landmine at once, and if it goes badly you've lost almost nothing. Want me to write that config delta?
what does codec do

The ES8311 is the analog↔digital bridge between your microphone/speaker and the ESP32. "Codec" here means **coder/decoder** in the hardware sense — not the software sense (MP3, Opus). Different thing entirely, and the name collision trips people up. Your tree has `external/opus`, which *is* the software kind: compression. The ES8311 does no compression at all.

## Why you need one

The ESP32-S3's I²S peripheral only speaks digital serial audio — a bit clock and a stream of ones and zeros. A microphone produces a few **millivolts** of wobbling analog voltage. Nothing in the SoC can read that. A speaker is the same problem backwards: it needs analog current, and the SoC only emits bits.

The codec sits in the middle and does the conversion both ways.

## What it actually does on your board

**Capture (what voice control needs):**

```
MIC (analog, ~mV, differential)
  → MIC1P / MIC1N            ES8311 pins 18/17
  → preamp                   gain is a register — ES8311_ADC_REG16
  → ADC                      analog → 16-bit samples, e.g. 16 kHz
  → I2S_ASDOUT (GPIO14)      digital stream → ESP32
```

**Playback:**

```
ESP32 → I2S_DSDIN (GPIO16)
  → DAC                      samples → analog
  → OUTP / OUTN              ES8311 pins 12/13
  → NS4150B amp              enable = PA_CTRL on expander EXIO7
  → speaker                  6Ω 1W, MX1.25 header
```

That amp is a separate chip and exists because the codec's output is line-level — far too weak to move a speaker cone.

## Two buses, two jobs

This is the part worth internalizing, since it explains the whole pin layout:

- **I²S (GPIO 12/13/14/15/16)** carries the *audio data*, continuously, at a fixed rate. MCLK (12) is the master clock that drives the converters themselves — that's why the codec is dead without it.
- **I²C (GPIO 7/8)** carries *control*: sample rate, mic gain, mute, data format. A handful of register writes at startup, then silence.

Same reason your camera has a DVP data bus and an I²C control line. Data path and control path are separate.

## In one line

Without the codec: your mic is an unreadable analog signal and your speaker is a dead coil. With it: `read()` on `/dev/audio0` returns PCM samples you can feed to a keyword-spotting model, and `write()` makes sound come out.

Note it's **mono** — one mic in, one speaker out. Perfectly fine for voice; you're not doing stereo anything.
so why record an audio instead of free speech

Because it isn't a feature — it's a multimeter.

Recording a `.wav` and playing it back tests the entire chain below the model in one shot: I²C register writes reaching the codec, MCLK actually clocking, I²S pins mapped right, DMA delivering buffers, sample rate and bit depth correct, the amp enable on EXIO7, and the physical mic being alive. If it plays back and sounds like you, **everything under the recognition layer is proven.**

## The alternative is the buzz saga again

Suppose you skip it and go straight at keyword spotting. The model outputs garbage. Now, what's broken?

- wrong I²S pins in defconfig
- MCLK not enabled
- sample rate mismatch (codec at 8 k, model expecting 16 k)
- mic gain too low — silence in, silence out
- wrong bit depth or byte order
- MFCC frontend bug
- the model itself is just bad

Seven suspects, none of them visible from the output. You'd be building and flashing against an invisible fault.

You've run this exact experiment already. Three coils were wired to pins that reach no header, and you burned many build/flash cycles sweeping coil-order tables — testing the *last* layer while the fault sat in the *first* one. The `.wav` is the cheap way to not repeat that.

## Audio faults are silent

This is what makes audio nastier than most bring-up. Nothing throws an error. Wrong sample rate gives you chipmunk playback. Wrong bit depth gives you white noise. Swapped byte order gives you a crackling roar. Mic gain at default gives you a file full of near-zeros that looks structurally perfect. Every one of these returns success from every API call.

They're invisible in code and *instantly obvious to an ear*. One second of listening replaces an afternoon of staring at buffers.

## And the recording isn't thrown away

You need audio of your own voice, through **this mic**, in **this enclosure**, to train and validate a keyword model. Mic frequency response, the plastic housing, room echo, the stepper's noise floor — a model trained on clean laptop recordings will underperform on this hardware. So the capture path you build for the smoke test is the same one that produces your dataset. It's step one of the real work, not a detour.

## On "free speech"

Worth separating: the `.wav` isn't standing in for free-form speech. Free-form speech isn't the next step, or any step, on-device — there's no ASR engine in the tree and no room for one. That path is cloud, via `bailian_sdk`.

But note the cloud path needs the *exact same thing*: capture clean PCM from the mic. So the `.wav` test is on the critical path either way. It's the one piece of work that isn't a bet.
